families.axis_name: From self-making independence to civic interdependence
families.decision_variable: When pursuing advancement, does he act mainly by self-directed personal maneuvering or by organizing coordinated public cooperation?

phase_contrasts.contrast: He shifts from escaping constraint through opportunistic self-authorship and flight to advancing through steadier self-discipline, reputation management, and practical self-reliance.
He shifts from mainly improving his own position through disciplined personal effort to pursuing goals by founding institutions and coordinating collective civic action.
He shifts from organizing local public projects and reforms to exercising the same cooperative mode through political mediation, negotiation, and coalition-building at a constitutional level.

0.rationale: In chapters 1–4, family control, apprenticeship, intensive self-education, and his escape from Boston fit a late-adolescent stage of striving for autonomy while still under household authority.

1.rationale: In chapters 5–9, his business advancement, marriage, and deliberate self-discipline mark early independent adulthood, even as he still depends on reputation and strategic relationships.

2.rationale: Across chapters 10–18, leading libraries, civic reforms, hospitals, academies, and scientific projects reflects established adult social authority exercised through institution-building and coordination.

3.rationale: In chapter 19, his role as a colonial agent and constitutional negotiator in London signals a later-life phase of senior public service, diplomacy, and coalition-building.

probes.scenario: In Boston, Benjamin's father presses to bind him to his brother James's printing house to cure his longing for the sea. The trade already pleases him more than candle-making, and books are beginning to open before him, but the indentures are now put before him.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin respond when his family moves to fix his future in the printing trade?

phase_responses.gt_action: He stands out for a time, then lets himself be persuaded and signs the indentures to his brother; afterward he throws himself into the trade and borrows books to read late at night.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He dislikes being bound, yet printing suits him better than his father's business and gives him books. Since he cannot choose freely, he turns the constraint into a private way of making himself.

voice.note: This fits young Franklin in Boston at chapter 2: the action matches his reluctant submission and eager self-education, and the thought is plausible in substance and tone, with no clear anachronism or knowledge beyond this point.

phase_fit.note: The response centers on accepting family/apprenticeship constraint while inwardly converting it into self-education and future self-authorship, which is characteristic of constrained youth rather than later practical or public modes.

phase_responses.gt_action: He accepts the binding and applies himself to learning the business well.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If I am bound, I may at least make something of it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The term goes against me, but the trade suits me better than my father's business. If I cannot choose freely yet, I can still grow expert, get books, and better my condition by diligence.

voice.note: The sentiment fits young Franklin, but it is phase-misaligned and too maturely retrospective for the Boston indenture scene, sounding more like the later self-reliant autobiographer of chapter 7 than the constrained youth who has not yet developed that steadier language of improving his condition by diligence.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames constraint as something to work within through diligence, skill-building, and self-improvement, which fits practical self-reliance more than mere youthful escape or later public coordination.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He accepts the binding with outward compliance and sets himself to master the business, using the shop and borrowed books to improve his skill and credit.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: If I must serve, I shall learn all I can by it.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: A fixed term is vexing, but railing will not mend it. Better to make himself useful, gain a reputation for industry, and draw every advantage he can from the place.

voice.note: The substance fits young Franklin, but the thought slips into third-person self-narration ('make himself useful') and sounds a shade too polished and retrospective for this earlier Boston moment.

phase_fit.note: The thought emphasizes tactical acceptance, self-improvement, industry, and reputation-building within constraint, which fits practical self-reliance more than mere youthful escape or later public coordination.

phase_responses.gt_action: He accepts the binding and settles to the printing house as useful work.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I was willing to like it better than the other trade.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He takes the constraint less as a private defeat than as a chance to be employed where books, papers, and capable men are at hand. If he must be fixed, let it be in a business that deals in things of use.

voice.note: The action and quoted speech fit the Boston apprenticeship scene, but the thought sounds too phase-2 Franklin—framing the indenture in terms of public usefulness, capable men, and things of use rather than the younger boy’s more immediate relief at escaping candle-making and gaining access to books.

phase_fit.note: The response accepts family-imposed apprenticeship and construes it as a tolerable opening for self-education through books and useful work, which matches constrained youth still operating within authority rather than later self-directed or public-coordinating agency.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He agrees to the apprenticeship and treats the printing house as a station from which to gather books, useful knowledge, and ties among booksellers and apprentices.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: This trade may make me useful, if I use it well.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: He sees the shop not only as his own ladder but as an entry into a world of print that joins people through shared knowledge. Even under restraint, he looks for how learning can circulate beyond himself.

voice.note: The response imports phase-2 Franklin’s mature civic language into an early Boston apprenticeship scene, especially in the thought about print 'joining people through shared knowledge' and learning 'circulat[ing] beyond himself,' which sounds too institution-minded and adult for that moment.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is his thought framing the printing trade not just as personal advancement but as a medium for circulating knowledge and connecting people, which aligns more with public usefulness and coordinated social benefit than mere self-reliance.

phase_responses.gt_action: He signs the indentures and submits the matter as a family settlement rather than a private defeat.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If this be judged best, I shall apply myself to it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He takes the binding less as a mere curb on his own wishes than as an arrangement among household authorities that ought, for the present, to stand. His mind turns to how a fixed place within that order may later let him serve with credit rather than break from it in heat.

voice.note: The language is period-plausible, but the thought is too late-Franklin in outlook—treating the indenture as a constitutional household settlement and imagining future service with credit rather than the younger Franklin’s resentment, ambition, and desire to escape constraint.

phase_fit.note: The response accepts family and apprenticeship authority as a legitimate household arrangement, showing a still-constrained youth who is authoring himself only within imposed structures rather than advancing through self-directed maneuvering or public coordination.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He signs with little show, preserving peace in the family, and applies himself to the trade while quietly enlarging his understanding through books and acquaintance.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: I will do my duty in it, and make the best use of it I can.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: Open resistance would spend influence to no purpose and harden others against him. Better to yield on the form, keep goodwill, and build room for future action through patience, competence, and connection.

voice.note: Though the outward compliance fits the situation, the thought sounds too late-Franklin and managerial for this Boston youth—phrases like 'spend influence,' 'build room for future action,' and 'connection' impose an older political mediator's calculus on an adolescent at the indentures.

phase_fit.note: The thought emphasizes tactically yielding, preserving goodwill, and using patience, competence, and relationships to create future room for advancement, which fits practical self-reliance more than mere constrained youth.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin is bound as an apprentice printer to his brother James, after resisting the arrangement and still feeling a pull toward the sea.
anchor_source.first_words: This bookish inclination at length determined my
anchor_source.last_words: early in the morning, lest it should
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
This bookish inclination at length determined my father to make me a
printer, though he had already one son (James) of that profession. In
1717 my brother James returned from England with a press and letters
to set up his business in Boston. I liked it much better than that of
my father, but still had a hankering for the sea. To prevent the
apprehended effect of such an inclination, my father was impatient to
have me bound to my brother. I stood out some time, but at last was
persuaded, and signed the indentures when I was yet but twelve years
old. I was to serve as an apprentice till I was twenty-one years of
age, only I was to be allowed journeyman's wages during the last year.
In a little time I made great proficiency in the business, and became
a useful hand to my brother. I now had access to better books. An
acquaintance with the apprentices of booksellers enabled me sometimes
to borrow a small one, which I was careful to return soon and clean.
Often I sat up in my room reading the greatest part of the night, when
the book was borrowed in the evening and to be returned early in the
morning, lest it should be missed or wanted.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the Boston apprenticeship setup with his father and brother James, and the response faithfully paraphrases that Franklin resisted for a time, was persuaded to sign the indentures, then advanced in printing and eagerly borrowed books to read at night; the thought is a reasonable inference from his stated preference for printing over his father's trade and his continued attraction to books despite being bound.

weak_pairs.note: Both phases answer the situation with essentially the same self-directed adaptation—accepting the indenture while privately converting constraint into personal improvement through diligence, expertise, and books.

Although Phase 2 uses slightly more 'useful' and socially tinged language, both responses still center on accepting the trade as a means of self-development rather than organizing coordinated public cooperation.

Both phases remain in a cooperative/embedded construal of the binding, but the difference is mostly tonal—useful placement versus family settlement and future service—rather than a clear shift on the self-maneuvering vs public-coordination axis.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are weakly differentiated here because the constrained family-apprenticeship scene keeps action nearly fixed, and the thought/speech shifts are too subtle to mark strong movement on the decision-variable axis.

probes.scenario: At a coffeehouse, several tradesmen complain that the town suffers from the same nuisance each season, yet each man waits for another to begin a remedy; one turns to Franklin and says a pen and a few sensible heads could set matters right. The table falls quiet, expecting him to propose the next step.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer this call to begin?

phase_responses.gt_action: He offers a neat written proposal of his own contriving and volunteers to draft it privately.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If the thing be well put, it may carry the rest.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He sees a chance to show his parts and make himself of consequence beyond his present station. Better to distinguish himself by wit and composition than be lost among older men’s delay.

voice.note: The language is period-appropriate and the motive fits young Franklin at this early stage: eager to advance by his pen, display his abilities, and rise above his subordinate station through private self-authorship rather than organized public leadership.

phase_fit.note: The response frames advancement as personal distinction through private drafting, wit, and reputation-building rather than organizing shared civic action, which best matches Franklin’s tactically self-directed practical self-reliance.

phase_responses.gt_action: He suggests a modest plan, sounding the men’s temper before naming what share he himself will undertake.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let us first see who will join in it, and on what terms.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He measures the company as much as the nuisance, knowing a good design miscarries if pushed ill. Advancement lies in appearing useful, prudent, and not too forward.

voice.note: This fits young Franklin’s chapter-7 phase well: the cautious, tactical proposal and inward attention to reputation, usefulness, and not being too forward sound period-appropriate and true to his practical self-reliance without invoking later civic-grandee habits.

phase_fit.note: The response emphasizes tact, sounding others out, and managing reputation—'appearing useful, prudent, and not too forward'—which fits practical self-reliance more than fully developed public coordination.

phase_responses.gt_action: He proposes a subscription and regular meeting, setting the matter into a standing scheme with shared duties.
phase_responses.gt_speech: A small contribution from many will do more than much talk from all.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He takes the complaint not as a single inconvenience but as raw material for a lasting public contrivance. The best remedy is one that teaches people to act together again when the next want appears.

voice.note: This fits Franklin in his civic-organizer phase: the subscription, regular meetings, and notion of turning a recurring nuisance into a durable public scheme sound period-appropriate, chapter-safe, and true to his habit of converting private complaint into coordinated usefulness.

phase_fit.note: The response frames advancement as creating a durable public institution—subscriptions, regular meetings, and shared duties—showing Franklin as a coordinator of collective civic action rather than a self-directed personal maneuverer.

phase_responses.gt_action: He draws the disputing men into agreement on a common paper fit to satisfy differing interests and move the town authorities.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let us frame it so every honest party may own some part of it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He reads the pause as a political moment: the obstacle is less the nuisance than divided interest and jealousies. A durable beginning must gather factions under one practicable expression.

voice.note: This fits late-phase Franklin well: the action, speech, and thought all sound like a seasoned mediator who turns private complaint into a jointly owned public measure, with period-plausible diction and no knowledge beyond chapter 19.

phase_fit.note: The thought construes the situation as one of divided interests and factional jealousies requiring a common expression that different parties can own, which is most diagnostic of Franklin's later political mediation mode.

world.note: The coffeehouse-and-tradesmen setup fits early-18th-century Boston/colonial life, uses only plausible period social tools, introduces no impossible characters or technologies, and presents a Franklin-appropriate noncanonical situation rather than reproducing a specific scene from chapter 2.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are adequately differentiated on the decision-variable axis: P0→P1 stays within self-directed advancement but shifts from self-display/private authorship to tactically calibrated self-reliance, P1→P2 clearly moves into organized collective cooperation, and P2→P3 remains cooperative while advancing to mediation among interests and coalition-building.

probes.scenario: After heavy rain, the village millrace has burst its bank and cut a channel through several fields. Neighbors crowd the breach, arguing over whose ground should be opened or spared, and all turn when Benjamin Franklin steps near.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer the quarrel at the broken bank?

phase_responses.gt_action: He studies the water's course and speaks up with a narrow fix that saves his household's plot first.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If the trench is cut here, the flood may turn before it ruins our row entirely.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He feels the press of elder voices and wants room to prove his own judgment. If he can show a clever remedy, he may escape being treated as merely a boy under command.

voice.note: The response fits an adolescent Franklin in an early colonial setting: the practical, self-advancing fix and desire to prove his judgment against elder authority are phase-appropriate, and the language is plain and non-anachronistic.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on pressure from elders, being treated as a boy, and using a clever fix to assert independence, which most strongly matches constrained youth seeking self-authorship under authority.

phase_responses.gt_action: He marks a practical line for a ditch and offers to help dig if the others will follow one plan.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Quarreling mends nothing; take this line, and I'll put my spade in with yours.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He sees that good sense must be joined to a useful manner if he means to be heeded. Advancement comes by showing himself steady, capable, and worth trusting in a pinch.

voice.note: The action, plain practical speech, and inward emphasis on steadiness, useful conduct, and earning trust fit young Franklin's phase-1 self-reliance, with no clear anachronism or knowledge beyond chapter 7.

phase_fit.note: Though he proposes a shared practical plan, his thought frames the moment mainly as proving himself steady, capable, and trustworthy for personal advancement, which fits practical self-reliance more than fully civic coordination.

phase_responses.gt_action: He sets the men to sections of the bank, assigns tools, and proposes a common work rota until the water is mastered.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let each man take a reach of bank; if we labor together, every field stands a better chance.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He reads the breach less as one man's loss than as a village problem needing order. The surest remedy is not his own labor alone, but a frame by which many hands can act together.

voice.note: This fits Franklin in his civic-organizer phase: the action, plain practical speech, and thought about creating an orderly scheme for many hands are era-appropriate, chapter-safe, and characteristic of his public usefulness.

phase_fit.note: The response construes the crisis as a shared civic problem and advances by organizing coordinated collective labor, which is the hallmark of Franklin's public-usefulness phase rather than personal maneuvering.

phase_responses.gt_action: He hears the chief claimants, frames a temporary sharing of damage and labor, and urges assent before work begins.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Save the bank first; reckon the burdens fairly after, with witnesses from both sides.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He knows a sound repair will fail if resentment hardens into factions. His mind goes to terms others can live under, so present necessity and future peace may stand together.

voice.note: The response fits late-phase Franklin as a practical mediator who seeks immediate public utility and a durable settlement, and its diction is plain, period-appropriate, and free of knowledge or tonal anachronism.

phase_fit.note: The response is most diagnostic of political mediation because he prioritizes immediate settlement through fair terms, witnesses, and preventing factional resentment by finding an arrangement both sides can live under.

world.note: The millrace-breach scenario stays within a generic pre-industrial agrarian setting with no source-world leakage, keeps Benjamin Franklin as protagonist, and the phase actions fit the required progression from adolescent self-assertion to young adult practicality, adult coordination, and older-adult mediation.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are separated on the decision variable: P0→P1 moves from self-proving, household-first maneuvering to steadier cooperative self-reliance; P1→P2 shifts clearly into organizing collective action; P2→P3 remains cooperative in both but differentiates from operational coordination into mediation and fair coalition management at a higher social-political level.

probes.scenario: In Philadelphia, talk runs hot over whether the province should issue more paper money: common people press for it, wealthy creditors resist it, and the matter has been argued among Franklin's companions. The dispute has gathered force, and Franklin has been much taken up with the question.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin respond when a public dispute has stirred him and he sees a chance to influence the matter?

phase_responses.gt_action: He listens rather than enters the dispute.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Such a public controversy lies beyond a boy still under apprenticeship and family direction. He would be more apt to take it in as matter for private reflection and future use than to think he could sway it now.

voice.note: This fits the early Franklin of chapters 1–2: observant, ambitious, and still socially subordinate, with no clear anachronism or knowledge beyond his youthful station, though the phrasing is slightly more editorial than vividly first-person.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames the controversy as something beyond someone still under apprenticeship and family authority, favoring private observation over any attempt to influence public affairs.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He writes a sharp anonymous piece arguing for the measure and gets it into print if he can.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: A printed argument is a way for a young man with little standing to make himself felt. If he cannot command men by place, he may slip past them by wit and the press.

voice.note: The impulse to use anonymous print and wit fits young Franklin, but at chapter 2 he is still a Boston apprentice and cannot plausibly be 'in Philadelphia' or be occupied with that later Pennsylvania paper-money controversy.

phase_fit.note: The response frames influence as a young man's tactical self-advancement through anonymous print, wit, and reputation-bypassing maneuver rather than through organizing collective civic cooperation or later political mediation.

phase_responses.gt_action: He writes and prints an anonymous pamphlet, "The Nature and Necessity of a Paper Currency," arguing for an addition.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The Junto debates have possessed him with the subject, and he is persuaded more currency will enlarge trade and employment. He sees that writing well can serve a public cause and also advance his own business.

voice.note: This fits Franklin in chapter 8: the anonymous pamphlet, his Junto-shaped interest in paper currency, and his mixed motive of public usefulness and prudent self-advancement all sound exactly like his practical, reputation-minded young-adult phase, with no anachronism or foreknowledge.

phase_fit.note: The response frames advancement as skilled personal maneuvering through anonymous persuasive writing that serves both a public issue and his own business, rather than primarily organizing collective civic cooperation.

phase_responses.gt_action: He drafts a persuasive piece for print, aiming to rally support by showing how the measure would help trade and the province at large.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He reads the dispute less as a private quarrel than as a question of public usefulness. What matters is to turn opinion toward a measure that will set more hands to work and strengthen the community.

voice.note: This fits Franklin in his civic-organizing phase: drafting a printed argument on paper currency as a matter of trade, employment, and public benefit is exactly the sort of publicly useful, coordinated reasoning he shows by chapter 14, and the diction is period-safe.

phase_fit.note: The response frames the issue in terms of public usefulness and shaping collective opinion for the province’s benefit, which fits Franklin as a coordinator of civic improvement more than a merely self-advancing tactician.

phase_responses.gt_action: He prepares a temperate anonymous paper that answers the creditors' fears while pressing the province's wider interest.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He treats the controversy as a matter to be composed, not merely won. The task is to frame the case so opposing interests can be brought to a settlement consistent with public credit and common benefit.

voice.note: This fits late-phase Franklin well: the anonymous, temperate pamphleteering and the thought of reconciling interests through public credit and common benefit sound period-appropriate, politically mediating, and fully within what chapter 19 Franklin would know and do.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is his thought that the dispute should be composed by framing a settlement between opposing interests for public benefit, which fits Franklin as a mediator rather than merely a self-advancing tactician or local civic organizer.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin writes an anonymous pamphlet supporting more paper currency, helps the measure pass, and is rewarded with profitable printing work for the government.
anchor_source.first_words: About this time there was a cry
anchor_source.last_words: in my hands as long as I follow'd the business.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
About this time there was a cry among the people for more paper money,
only fifteen thousand pounds being extant in the province, and that
soon to be sunk.[59] The wealthy inhabitants oppos'd any addition,
being against all paper currency, from an apprehension that it would
depreciate, as it had done in New England, to the prejudice of all
creditors. We had discuss'd this point in our Junto, where I was on
the side of an addition, being persuaded that the first small sum
struck in 1723 had done much good by increasing the trade, employment,
and number of inhabitants in the province, since I now saw all the old
houses inhabited, and many new ones building: whereas I remembered
well, that when I first walk'd about the streets of Philadelphia,
eating my roll, I saw most of the houses in Walnut Street, between
Second and Front streets,[60] with bills on their doors, "To be let";
and many likewise in Chestnut-street and other streets, which made me
then think the inhabitants of the city were deserting it one after
another.

Our debates possess'd me so fully of the subject, that I wrote and
printed an anonymous pamphlet on it, entitled "_The Nature and
Necessity of a Paper Currency_." It was well receiv'd by the common
people in general; but the rich men dislik'd it, for it increas'd and
strengthen'd the clamor for more money, and they happening to have no
writers among them that were able to answer it, their opposition
slacken'd, and the point was carried by a majority in the House. My
friends there, who conceiv'd I had been of some service, thought fit
to reward me by employing me in printing the money; a very profitable
jobb and a great help to me. This was another advantage gain'd by my
being able to write.

The utility of this currency became by time and experience so evident
as never afterwards to be much disputed; so that it grew soon to
fifty-five thousand pounds, and in 1739 to eighty thousand pounds,
since which it arose during war to upwards of three hundred and fifty
thousand pounds, trade, building, and inhabitants all the while
increasing, tho' I now think there are limits beyond which the
quantity may be hurtful.[61]

I soon after obtain'd, thro' my friend Hamilton, the printing of the
Newcastle paper money, another profitable jobb as I then thought it;
small things appearing great to those in small circumstances; and
these, to me, were really great advantages, as they were great
encouragements. He procured for me, also, the printing of the laws and
votes of that government, which continu'd in my hands as long as I
follow'd the business.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the Philadelphia paper-money controversy and Junto debates, and Franklin’s response is faithfully rendered as writing and printing the anonymous pamphlet in favor of more currency, with the thought about being persuaded by the debates and later seeing writing help both public aims and his business reasonably inferred from the passage.

weak_pairs.note: Both phases respond by writing a persuasive public piece to influence opinion, and while Phase 2 frames it more in terms of public usefulness, the action and decision mode remain largely the same rather than clearly shifting to organized collective coordination.

Both phases use essentially the same cooperative print-based intervention, with Phase 3 adding a more mediating, settlement-oriented thought style but not a strongly distinct move on the self-directed-versus-coordinated-public-cooperation axis.

discrimination.note: P0→P1 is clearly separated, but P1→P2 and P2→P3 overlap because all three later responses rely on persuasive authorship rather than distinctly different forms of coordinated public organization.

probes.scenario: At a coffee-house, several tradesmen complain that poor night watch and a recent small fire have put the street in danger. One turns to Franklin, saying he writes plainly and knows many sorts of men, and asks whether he will set on foot some remedy.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer this call in the moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: He offers a few practical notions, then keeps chiefly to observing who may be useful to know.
phase_responses.gt_speech: A better watch would do good; but I am yet too young to lead such a matter.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He feels the want is real, yet he has little standing and must first make his own way. Such talk is also a chance to show sense and be marked by men above him.

voice.note: This fits the young Franklin of the early chapters: cautious, observant, ambitious, and conscious of his low standing, with plain period-appropriate wording and no knowledge beyond his station.

phase_fit.note: His thought centers on limited standing, making his own way, and using the moment to display sense and cultivate advantageous connections, which fits practical self-reliant advancement more than coordinated public action.

phase_responses.gt_action: He proposes to draft a short paper and sound discreet men privately before engaging himself further.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If the thing be useful, I can put the case in a plain light and learn who will join it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He reads this as a test of judgment and credit, not merely zeal. Better to proceed by pen, tact, and reputation than to be caught in a noisy scheme resting on other men's heat.

voice.note: This fits phase-1 Franklin well: the plain, useful phrasing and the inward emphasis on credit, discretion, pen, and avoiding rash public heat sound like his young-adult prudence without invoking later civic-institution language or any anachronism.

phase_fit.note: The response frames advancement as a matter of cautious personal judgment, pen, tact, and reputation management rather than openly organizing a collective institution, which is most characteristic of practical self-reliance.

phase_responses.gt_action: He invites the company to meet, subscribe rules, and choose officers for a regular watch and fire-assistance society.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let us reduce it to method, and each man bear a part; then the thing may last.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He sees a common inconvenience best cured by a standing contrivance, not by scattered complaints. His mind turns from his own part to framing a durable association others can carry with him.

voice.note: This fits Franklin in his civic-organizing phase: the plain, methodical proposal of rules, officers, and a lasting association is era-appropriate, chapter-safe, and true to his turn from private advancement toward coordinated public usefulness.

phase_fit.note: The response frames advancement through creating a durable, rule-governed civic association in which others share roles, which is quintessentially Franklin's public-usefulness and coordinated-action phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: He draws the disputing parties into calmer talk and proposes a paper fit to unite householders, magistrates, and tradesmen.
phase_responses.gt_speech: We shall do more by bringing the interests together than by charging one another with neglect.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He construes the danger as partly civic and partly political, since remedies fail when parties take alarm or offense. The useful course is to reconcile interests and shape a proposal many hands can own.

voice.note: This fits late-phase Franklin well: the plain, conciliatory speech and the thought about reconciling interests through a jointly owned proposal sound like his mature habit of public mediation, with no clear anachronism or knowledge beyond chapter 19.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on reconciling offended parties, aligning magistrates and householders, and crafting a proposal many interests can jointly own, which is most diagnostic of Franklin's later political mediation rather than merely civic project coordination.

world.note: The coffee-house complaint is plausible for Franklin’s Philadelphia world around chapter 7, uses only period-appropriate civic concerns and methods, introduces no impossible characters or technologies, and does not recreate a specific canonical scene.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses answer advancement through coordinated public cooperation, with Phase 2 building a durable civic association and Phase 3 mediating among stakeholders within the same cooperative mode rather than shifting the decision-variable axis.

discrimination.note: P0→P1 is separated by a move from hesitant self-positioning and observation to deliberate self-reliant maneuvering through tact and reputation, and P1→P2 is separated by a clear shift from personal advancement via disciplined private initiative to institution-building and organized collective action.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Peace being concluded, and the association business therefore at an
end, I turn'd my thoughts again to the affair of establishing an
academy. The first step I took was to associate in the design a number
of active friends, of whom the Junto furnished a good part; the next
was to write and publish a pamphlet, entitled _Proposals Relating to
the Education of Youth in Pennsylvania_. This I distributed among the
principal inhabitants gratis; and as soon as I could suppose their
minds a little prepared by the perusal of it, I set on foot a
subscription for opening and supporting an academy; it was to be paid
in quotas yearly for five years; by so dividing it, I judg'd the
subscription might be larger, and I believe it was so, amounting to no
less, if I remember right, than five thousand pounds.

In the introduction to these proposals, I stated their publication,
not as an act of mine, but of some _publick-spirited gentlemen_,
avoiding as much as I could, according to my usual rule, the
presenting myself to the publick as the author of any scheme for their
benefit.

The subscribers, to carry the project into immediate execution, chose
out of their number twenty-four trustees, and appointed Mr.
Francis,[86] then attorney-general, and myself to draw up constitutions
for the government of the academy; which being done and signed, a
house was hired, masters engag'd, and the schools opened, I think, in
the same year, 1749.

The scholars increasing fast, the house was soon found too small, and
we were looking out for a piece of ground, properly situated, with
intention to build, when Providence threw into our way a large house
ready built, which, with a few alterations, might well serve our
purpose. This was the building before mentioned, erected by the
hearers of Mr. Whitefield, and was obtained for us in the following
manner.

The trustees of the academy, after a while, were incorporated by a
charter from the governor; their funds were increas'd by contributions
in Britain and grants of land from the proprietaries, to which the
Assembly has since made considerable addition; and thus was
established the present University of Philadelphia.[87] I have been
continued one of its trustees from the beginning, now near forty
years, and have had the very great pleasure of seeing a number of the
youth who have receiv'd their education in it, distinguish'd by their
improv'd abilities, serviceable in public stations, and ornaments to
their country.

probes.scenario: In Philadelphia, Governor Keith warmly offers to set Franklin up in business, asks for an inventory of printing supplies from England, and suggests Franklin himself go over to choose them and make useful connections. phase_responses.gt_speech: I agreed that this might be advantageous.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The governor's cordial manner seems proof enough of sincerity. Unasked generosity from a man of rank feels like honest patronage, and I take his promise as the natural opening of my fortune.

anchor_source.event_description: Sir William Keith continues to flatter Franklin and promises to order printing equipment from England, leading Franklin to trust him completely and plan a trip to England to choose the materials himself.
anchor_source.first_words: The breaking into this money of
anchor_source.last_words: did not happen for some years after.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
The breaking into this money of Vernon's was one of the first great
errata of my life; and this affair show'd that my father was not much
out in his judgment when he suppos'd me too young to manage business
of importance. But Sir William, on reading his letter, said he was too
prudent. There was great difference in persons; and discretion did not
always accompany years, nor was youth always without it. "And since he
will not set you up," says he, "I will do it myself. Give me an
inventory of the things necessary to be had from England, and I will
send for them. You shall repay me when you are able; I am resolv'd to
have a good printer here, and I am sure you must succeed." This was
spoken with such an appearance of cordiality, that I had not the least
doubt of his meaning what he said. I had hitherto kept the proposition
of my setting up, a secret in Philadelphia, and I still kept it. Had
it been known that I depended on the governor, probably some friend,
that knew him better, would have advis'd me not to rely on him, as I
afterwards heard it as his known character to be liberal of promises
which he never meant to keep. Yet, unsolicited as he was by me, how
could I think his generous offers insincere? I believ'd him one of the
best men in the world.

I presented him an inventory of a little print'-house, amounting by my
computation to about one hundred pounds sterling. He lik'd it, but
ask'd me if my being on the spot in England to chuse the types, and
see that everything was good of the kind, might not be of some
advantage. "Then," says he, "when there, you may make acquaintances,
and establish correspondences in the bookselling and stationery way."
I agreed that this might be advantageous. "Then," says he, "get
yourself ready to go with Annis;" which was the annual ship, and the
only one at that time usually passing between London and Philadelphia.
But it would be some months before Annis sail'd, so I continued
working with Keimer, fretting about the money Collins had got from me,
and in daily apprehensions of being call'd upon by Vernon, which,
however, did not happen for some years after.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the Philadelphia exchange with Governor Keith, the action and quoted speech track Franklin’s actual response that he presented an inventory and agreed the England trip might be advantageous, and the thought is directly supported by his stated lack of doubt in Keith’s sincerity and belief that his generous patronage was genuine.

probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer this offer under the merchants' eyes?

phase_responses.gt_action: He accepts the gentleman's hand and agrees to go, asking only when he should be ready.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Sir, I am much obliged to you, and shall be ready at the time you appoint.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A man of figure would not lightly offer his countenance before other merchants. If he sees something in me, good conduct and industry may well carry me upward.

voice.note: This fits early Franklin well: the deferential speech, readiness to trust a gentleman's public countenance, and belief that industry plus patronage will advance him are all apt to chapter 2 and free of anachronism.

phase_responses.gt_action: He thanks the gentleman but asks for the terms in writing before giving his word.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I am thankful for your good opinion; pray let me see the terms plain, and then I shall answer you.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Fair words cost little, and a public air may hide an empty promise. I have been too easy before; better to seem cautious than be left to mend another erratum.

phase_responses.gt_speech: If the matter be real, let us have the business opened plainly—service, wages, and who stands engaged for payment.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Credit rests on known terms, not on compliments. Since others are present, the offer should bear open examination; if it shrinks from that, it is not fit to build upon.

voice.note: This fits Franklin’s chapter-13 prudence well: the language is period-appropriate, the insistence on plain terms and accountable payment suits his institutional caution, and nothing reaches beyond what he could know at that point.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin revises his religious and moral outlook, moving from youthful Deism toward a practical ethic centered on truth, sincerity, and integrity.
anchor_source.first_words: Before I enter upon my public appearance
anchor_source.last_words: I valued it properly, and determin'd to preserve it.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Before I enter upon my public appearance in business, it may be well
to let you know the then state of my mind with regard to my principles
and morals, that you may see how far those influenc'd the future
events of my life. My parents had early given me religious
impressions, and brought me through my childhood piously in the
Dissenting way. But I was scarce fifteen, when, after doubting by
turns of several points, as I found them disputed in the different
books I read, I began to doubt of Revelation itself. Some books
against Deism[52] fell into my hands; they were said to be the
substance of sermons preached at Boyle's Lectures. It happened that
they wrought an effect on me quite contrary to what was intended by
them; for the arguments of the Deists, which were quoted to be
refuted, appeared to me much stronger than the refutations; in short,
I soon became a thorough Deist. My arguments perverted some others,
particularly Collins and Ralph; but, each of them having afterwards
wrong'd me greatly without the least compunction, and recollecting
Keith's conduct towards me (who was another free-thinker), and my own
towards Vernon and Miss Read, which at times gave me great trouble, I
began to suspect that this doctrine, tho' it might be true, was not
very useful. My London pamphlet, which had for its motto these lines
of Dryden:[53]

  "Whatever is, is right. Though purblind man
   Sees but a part o' the chain, the nearest link:
   His eyes not carrying to the equal beam,
   That poises all above;"

and from the attributes of God, his infinite wisdom, goodness and
power, concluded that nothing could possibly be wrong in the world,
and that vice and virtue were empty distinctions, no such things
existing, appear'd now not so clever a performance as I once thought
it; and I doubted whether some error had not insinuated itself
unperceiv'd into my argument, so as to infect all that follow'd, as is
common in metaphysical reasonings.

    [52] The creed of an eighteenth century theological sect
    which, while believing in God, refused to credit the
    possibility of miracles and to acknowledge the validity
    of revelation.

    [53] A great English poet, dramatist, and critic
    (1631-1700). The lines are inaccurately quoted from
    Dryden's OEdipus, Act III, Scene I, line 293.

I grew convinc'd that _truth_, _sincerity_ and _integrity_ in dealings
between man and man were of the utmost importance to the felicity of
life; and I form'd written resolutions, which still remain in my
journal book, to practice them ever while I lived. Revelation had
indeed no weight with me, as such; but I entertain'd an opinion that,
though certain actions might not be bad _because_ they were forbidden
by it, or good _because_ it commanded them, yet probably these actions
might be forbidden _because_ they were bad for us, or commanded
_because_ they were beneficial to us, in their own natures, all the
circumstances of things considered. And this persuasion, with the kind
hand of Providence, or some guardian angel, or accidental favourable
circumstances and situations, or all together, preserved me, thro'
this dangerous time of youth, and the hazardous situations I was
sometimes in among strangers, remote from the eye and advice of my
father, without any willful gross immorality or injustice, that might
have been expected from my want of religion. I say willful, because
the instances I have mentioned had something of _necessity_ in them,
from my youth, inexperience, and the knavery of others. I had
therefore a tolerable character to begin the world with; I valued it
properly, and determin'd to preserve it.

anchor.note: The scenario fits Franklin’s retrospective self-examination, and the response faithfully reflects that he doubts his earlier metaphysical argument, concludes truth, sincerity, and integrity are essential, writes resolutions to practice them, and determines to preserve his character, with no invented speech.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses answer with nearly the same practical turn toward honesty and written self-correction, with Phase 1 only slightly more suspicious of error and deceit rather than clearly requiring proof, terms, or safeguards before commitment.

Phase 2 sounds somewhat more rule- and conduct-oriented, but both phases still frame the issue mainly as personal moral discipline and judging by practical effects rather than a distinct shift to explicit external safeguards or verifiable commitments.

discrimination.note: Across all three phases, the scene elicits a stable resolution toward honesty and practical moral rules, so the adjacent contrasts on the trust-versus-safeguards axis are only weakly expressed in thought.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin's business prospers, his newspaper becomes highly profitable, and he expands his printing partnerships by establishing former workmen in other colonies under carefully explicit agreements.
anchor_source.first_words: My business was now continually augmenting, and
anchor_source.last_words: perhaps with lawsuits and other disagreeable consequences.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
My business was now continually augmenting, and my circumstances
growing daily easier, my newspaper having become very profitable, as
being for a time almost the only one in this and the neighbouring
provinces. I experienced, too, the truth of the observation, "_that
after getting the first hundred pound, it is more easy to get the
second_," money itself being of a prolific nature.

The partnership at Carolina having succeeded, I was encourag'd to
engage in others, and to promote several of my workmen, who had
behaved well, by establishing them with printing-houses in different
colonies, on the same terms with that in Carolina. Most of them did
well, being enabled at the end of our term, six years, to purchase the
types of me and go on working for themselves, by which means several
families were raised. Partnerships often finish in quarrels; but I was
happy in this, that mine were all carried on and ended amicably,
owing, I think, a good deal to the precaution of having very
explicitly settled, in our articles, everything to be done by or
expected from each partner, so that there was nothing to dispute,
which precaution I would therefore recommend to all who enter into
partnerships; for, whatever esteem partners may have for, and
confidence in each other at the time of the contract, little
jealousies and disgusts may arise, with ideas of inequality in the
care and burden of the business, etc., which are attended often with
breach of friendship and of the connection, perhaps with lawsuits and
other disagreeable consequences.

anchor.note: The scenario matches Franklin’s profitable business and his establishing well-behaved workmen in other colonies, and the action, quoted speech, and inferred thought all faithfully reflect his stated precaution of explicitly settling partnership articles because mutual esteem and confidence are not enough to prevent later jealousy and disputes.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin writes anonymous pieces for the New England Courant, receives praise from his brother's literary circle, and feels intense vanity at being mistaken for a more accomplished writer.
anchor_source.first_words: He had some ingenious men among
anchor_source.last_words: it, which at length offered in
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
He had some ingenious men among his friends, who amus'd themselves by
writing little pieces for this paper, which gain'd it credit and made
it more in demand, and these gentlemen often visited us. Hearing their
conversations, and their accounts of the approbation their papers were
received with, I was excited to try my hand among them; but, being
still a boy, and suspecting that my brother would object to printing
anything of mine in his paper if he knew it to be mine, I contrived to
disguise my hand, and, writing an anonymous paper, I put it in at
night under the door of the printing-house. It was found in the
morning, and communicated to his writing friends when they call'd in
as usual. They read it, commented on it in my hearing, and I had the
exquisite pleasure of finding it met with their approbation, and that,
in their different guesses at the author, none were named but men of
some character among us for learning and ingenuity. I suppose now that
I was rather lucky in my judges, and that perhaps they were not really
so very good ones as I then esteem'd them.

Encourag'd, however, by this, I wrote and conveyed in the same way to
the press several more papers which were equally approv'd; and I kept
my secret till my small fund of sense for such performances was pretty
well exhausted, and then I discovered[24] it, when I began to be
considered a little more by my brother's acquaintance, and in a manner
that did not quite please him, as he thought, probably with reason,
that it tended to make me too vain. And, perhaps, this might be one
occasion of the differences that we began to have about this time.
Though a brother, he considered himself as my master, and me as his
apprentice, and, accordingly, expected the same services from me as he
would from another, while I thought he demean'd me too much in some he
requir'd of me, who from a brother expected more indulgence. Our
disputes were often brought before our father, and I fancy I was
either generally in the right, or else a better pleader, because the
judgment was generally in my favor. But my brother was passionate,
and had often beaten me, which I took extreamly amiss; and, thinking
my apprenticeship very tedious, I was continually wishing for some
opportunity of shortening it, which at length offered in a manner
unexpected.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the printing-house setup and his fear of his brother’s refusal, the action faithfully paraphrases his anonymous nighttime submission with no invented speech, and the thought is supported by the text’s statements that he was excited to try, enjoyed the secret approbation, and took pleasure in being mistaken for learned men.

weak_pairs.note: Both choose the same anonymous submission tactic and both still center the hidden pleasure of proving his cleverness, with Phase 1 adding only mild self-conscious caution about seeming forward.

The action remains identical and the thought shift from avoiding forward self-promotion to wanting the writing judged on its merits is subtle rather than a clear move to usefulness/results carrying the claim.

discrimination.note: All three responses use the same unsigned-submission strategy, and the phase signal appears only as modest differences in inner framing rather than strong adjacent differentiation on visible self-display versus muted, usefulness-centered pursuit.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin adds humility to his list of virtues after a Quaker friend tells him he is widely perceived as proud, overbearing, and too eager to be right.
anchor_source.first_words: My list of virtues contain'd at first
anchor_source.last_words: probably be proud of my humility.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
My list of virtues contain'd at first but twelve; but a Quaker friend
having kindly informed me that I was generally thought proud; that my
pride show'd itself frequently in conversation; that I was not content
with being in the right when discussing any point, but was
overbearing, and rather insolent, of which he convinc'd me by
mentioning several instances; I determined endeavouring to cure
myself, if I could, of this vice or folly among the rest, and I added
_Humility_ to my list, giving an extensive meaning to the word.

I cannot boast of much success in acquiring the _reality_ of this
virtue, but I had a good deal with regard to the _appearance_ of it. I
made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction to the sentiments
of others, and all positive assertion of my own. I even forbid myself,
agreeably to the old laws of our Junto, the use of every word or
expression in the language that imported a fix'd opinion, such as
_certainly, undoubtedly_, etc., and I adopted, instead of them, _I
conceive, I apprehend_, or _I imagine_ a thing to be so or so; or it
_so appears to me at present_. When another asserted something that I
thought an error, I deny'd myself the pleasure of contradicting him
abruptly, and of showing immediately some absurdity in his
proposition; and in answering I began by observing that in certain
cases or circumstances his opinion would be right, but in the present
case there _appear'd_ or _seem'd_ to me some difference, etc. I soon
found the advantage of this change in my manner; the conversations I
engag'd in went on more pleasantly. The modest way in which I propos'd
my opinions procur'd them a readier reception and less contradiction;
I had less mortification when I was found to be in the wrong, and I
more easily prevail'd with others to give up their mistakes and join
with me when I happened to be in the right.

And this mode, which I at first put on with some violence to natural
inclination, became at length so easy, and so habitual to me, that
perhaps for these fifty years past no one has ever heard a dogmatical
expression escape me. And to this habit (after my character of
integrity) I think it principally owing that I had early so much
weight with my fellow-citizens when I proposed new institutions, or
alterations in the old, and so much influence in public councils when
I became a member; for I was but a bad speaker, never eloquent,
subject to much hesitation in my choice of words, hardly correct in
language, and yet I generally carried my points.

In reality, there is, perhaps, no one of our natural passions so hard
to subdue as _pride_. Disguise it, struggle with it, beat it down,
stifle it, mortify it as much as one pleases, it is still alive, and
will every now and then peep out and show itself; you will see it,
perhaps, often in this history; for, even if I could conceive that I
had compleatly overcome it, I should probably be proud of my humility.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
In 1751, Dr. Thomas Bond, a particular friend of mine, conceived the
idea of establishing a hospital in Philadelphia (a very beneficent
design, which has been ascrib'd to me, but was originally his), for
the reception and cure of poor sick persons, whether inhabitants of
the province or strangers. He was zealous and active in endeavouring
to procure subscriptions for it, but the proposal being a novelty in
America, and at first not well understood, he met but with small
success.

At length he came to me with the compliment that he found there was no
such thing as carrying a public-spirited project through without my
being concern'd in it. "For," says he, "I am often ask'd by those to
whom I propose subscribing, Have you consulted Franklin upon this
business? And what does he think of it? And when I tell them that I
have not (supposing it rather out of your line), they do not
subscribe, but say they will consider of it." I enquired into the
nature and probable utility of his scheme, and receiving from him a
very satisfactory explanation, I not only subscrib'd to it myself, but
engag'd heartily in the design of procuring subscriptions from others.
Previously, however, to the solicitation, I endeavoured to prepare the
minds of the people by writing on the subject in the newspapers, which
was my usual custom in such cases, but which he had omitted.

The subscriptions afterwards were more free and generous; but,
beginning to flag, I saw they would be insufficient without some
assistance from the Assembly, and therefore propos'd to petition for
it, which was done. The country members did not at first relish the
project; they objected that it could only be serviceable to the city,
and therefore the citizens alone should be at the expense of it; and
they doubted whether the citizens themselves generally approv'd of it.
My allegation on the contrary, that it met with such approbation as to
leave no doubt of our being able to raise two thousand pounds by
voluntary donations, they considered as a most extravagant
supposition, and utterly impossible.

On this I form'd my plan; and, asking leave to bring in a bill for
incorporating the contributors according to the prayer of their
petition, and granting them a blank sum of money, which leave was
obtained chiefly on the consideration that the House could throw the
bill out if they did not like it, I drew it so as to make the
important clause a conditional one, viz., "And be it enacted, by the
authority aforesaid, that when the said contributors shall have met
and chosen their managers and treasurer, _and shall have raised by
their contributions a capital stock of----value_ (the yearly
interest of which is to be applied to the accommodating of the
sick poor in the said hospital, free of charge for diet, attendance,
advice, and medicines), _and shall make the same appear to the
satisfaction of the speaker of the Assembly for the time being_, that
_then_ it shall and may be lawful for the said speaker, and he is
hereby required, to sign an order on the provincial treasurer for the
payment of two thousand pounds, in two yearly payments, to the
treasurer of the said hospital, to be applied to the founding,
building, and finishing of the same."

This condition carried the bill through; for the members, who had
oppos'd the grant, and now conceiv'd they might have the credit of
being charitable without the expense, agreed to its passage; and then,
in soliciting subscriptions among the people, we urg'd the conditional
promise of the law as an additional motive to give, since every man's
donation would be doubled; thus the clause work'd both ways. The
subscriptions accordingly soon exceeded the requisite sum, and we
claim'd and receiv'd the public gift, which enabled us to carry the
design into execution. A convenient and handsome building was soon
erected; the institution has by constant experience been found useful,
and flourishes to this day; and I do not remember any of my political
manoeuvers, the success of which gave me at the time more pleasure,
or wherein, after thinking of it, I more easily excus'd myself for
having made some use of cunning.

anchor.note: The scenario accurately captures Bond’s appeal, the public and Assembly hesitation, and Franklin’s involvement, while the response faithfully paraphrases Franklin’s actual actions and reasonably infers his utility-testing and self-excused “cunning” from the passage.

anchor_source.event_description: As a boy, Franklin leads other children in secretly taking stones to build a wharf for fishing, but the theft is discovered and he is corrected by his father, leading him to conclude that usefulness does not justify dishonesty.
anchor_source.first_words: I disliked the trade, and had
anchor_source.last_words: better instructed, tastes and appetites.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
I disliked the trade, and had a strong inclination for the sea, but my
father declared against it; however, living near the water, I was much
in and about it, learnt early to swim well, and to manage boats; and
when in a boat or canoe with other boys, I was commonly allowed to
govern, especially in any case of difficulty; and upon other occasions
I was generally a leader among the boys, and sometimes led them into
scrapes, of which I will mention one instance, as it shows an early
projecting public spirit, tho' not then justly conducted.

There was a salt-marsh that bounded part of the mill-pond, on the edge
of which, at high water, we used to stand to fish for minnows. By much
trampling, we had made it a mere quagmire. My proposal was to build a
wharf there fit for us to stand upon, and I showed my comrades a large
heap of stones, which were intended for a new house near the marsh,
and which would very well suit our purpose. Accordingly, in the
evening, when the workmen were gone, I assembled a number of my
playfellows, and working with them diligently like so many emmets,
sometimes two or three to a stone, we brought them all away and built
our little wharf. The next morning the workmen were surprised at
missing the stones, which were found in our wharf. Inquiry was made
after the removers; we were discovered and complained of; several of
us were corrected by our fathers; and, though I pleaded the usefulness
of the work, mine convinced me that nothing was useful which was not
honest.

I think you may like to know something of his person and character. He
had an excellent constitution of body, was of middle stature, but well
set, and very strong; he was ingenious, could draw prettily, was
skilled a little in music, and had a clear, pleasing voice, so that
when he played psalm tunes on his violin and sung withal, as he
sometimes did in an evening after the business of the day was over, it
was extremely agreeable to hear. He had a mechanical genius too, and,
on occasion, was very handy in the use of other tradesmen's tools; but
his great excellence lay in a sound understanding and solid judgment
in prudential matters, both in private and publick affairs. In the
latter, indeed, he was never employed, the numerous family he had to
educate and the straitness of his circumstances keeping him close to
his trade; but I remember well his being frequently visited by leading
people, who consulted him for his opinion in affairs of the town or of
the church he belonged to, and showed a good deal of respect for his
judgment and advice: he was also much consulted by private persons
about their affairs when any difficulty occurred, and frequently
chosen an arbitrator between contending parties. At his table he liked
to have, as often as he could, some sensible friend or neighbor to
converse with, and always took care to start some ingenious or useful
topic for discourse, which might tend to improve the minds of his
children. By this means he turned our attention to what was good,
just, and prudent in the conduct of life; and little or no notice was
ever taken of what related to the victuals on the table, whether it
was well or ill dressed, in or out of season, of good or bad flavor,
preferable or inferior to this or that other thing of the kind, so
that I was bro't up in such a perfect inattention to those matters as
to be quite indifferent what kind of food was set before me, and so
unobservant of it, that to this day if I am asked I can scarce tell a
few hours after dinner what I dined upon. This has been a convenience
to me in traveling, where my companions have been sometimes very
unhappy for want of a suitable gratification of their more delicate,
because better instructed, tastes and appetites.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin conceives an ambitious project of achieving moral perfection and begins systematically testing himself against thirteen virtues using a daily bookkeeping method.
anchor_source.first_words: It was about this time I
anchor_source.last_words: respecting that virtue upon that day.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
It was about this time I conceived the bold and arduous project of
arriving at moral perfection. I wish'd to live without committing any
fault at any time; I would conquer all that either natural
inclination, custom, or company might lead me into. As I knew, or
thought I knew, what was right and wrong, I did not see why I might
not always do the one and avoid the other. But I soon found I had
undertaken a task of more difficulty than I had imagined.[66] While my
care was employ'd in guarding against one fault, I was often surprised
by another; habit took the advantage of inattention; inclination was
sometimes too strong for reason. I concluded, at length, that the mere
speculative conviction that it was our interest to be completely
virtuous, was not sufficient to prevent our slipping; and that the
contrary habits must be broken, and good ones acquired and
established, before we can have any dependence on a steady, uniform
rectitude of conduct. For this purpose I therefore contrived the
following method.

    [66] Compare Philippians iv, 8.

In the various enumerations of the moral virtues I had met with in my
reading, I found the catalogue more or less numerous, as different
writers included more or fewer ideas under the same name. Temperance,
for example, was by some confined to eating and drinking, while by
others it was extended to mean the moderating every other pleasure,
appetite, inclination, or passion, bodily or mental, even to our
avarice and ambition. I propos'd to myself, for the sake of clearness,
to use rather more names, with fewer ideas annex'd to each, than a few
names with more ideas; and I included under thirteen names of virtues
all that at that time occurr'd to me as necessary or desirable, and
annexed to each a short precept, which fully express'd the extent I
gave to its meaning.

These names of virtues, with their precepts, were:

1. Temperance.

Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation.

2. Silence.

Speak not but what may benefit others or yourself; avoid trifling
conversation.

3. Order.

Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business
have its time.

4. Resolution.

Resolve to perform what you ought; perform without fail what you
resolve.

5. Frugality.

Make no expense but to do good to others or yourself; _i. e._, waste
nothing.

6. INDUSTRY.

Lose no time; be always employ'd in something useful; cut off all
unnecessary actions.

7. Sincerity.

Use no hurtful deceit; think innocently and justly; and, if you speak,
speak accordingly.

8. Justice.

Wrong none by doing injuries, or omitting the benefits that are your
duty.

9. Moderation.

Avoid extreams; forbear resenting injuries so much as you think they
deserve.

10. Cleanliness.

Tolerate no uncleanliness in body, cloaths, or habitation.

11. Tranquillity.

Be not disturbed at trifles, or at accidents common or unavoidable.

12. Chastity.

Rarely use venery but for Health or Offspring; Never to Dulness, Weakness, or the Injury of your own or another's Peace or Reputation.

13. Humility.

Imitate Jesus and Socrates.

My intention being to acquire the _habitude_ of all these virtues, I
judg'd it would be well not to distract my attention by attempting the
whole at once, but to fix it on one of them at a time; and, when I
should be master of that, then to proceed to another, and so on, till
I should have gone thro' the thirteen; and, as the previous
acquisition of some might facilitate the acquisition of certain
others, I arrang'd them with that view, as they stand above.
Temperance first, as it tends to procure that coolness and clearness
of head, which is so necessary where constant vigilance was to be kept
up, and guard maintained against the unremitting attraction of ancient
habits, and the force of perpetual temptations. This being acquir'd
and establish'd, Silence would be more easy; and my desire being to
gain knowledge at the same time that I improv'd in virtue, and
considering that in conversation it was obtain'd rather by the use of
the ears than of the tongue, and therefore wishing to break a habit I
was getting into of prattling, punning, and joking, which only made me
acceptable to trifling company, I gave _Silence_ the second place.
This and the next, _Order_, I expected would allow me more time for
attending to my project and my studies. _Resolution_, once become
habitual, would keep me firm in my endeavours to obtain all the
subsequent virtues; _Frugality_ and Industry freeing me from my
remaining debt, and producing affluence and independence, would make
more easy the practice of Sincerity and Justice, etc., etc. Conceiving
then, that, agreeably to the advice of Pythagoras[67] in his Golden
Verses, daily examination would be necessary, I contrived the
following method for conducting that examination.

I made a little book, in which I allotted a page for each of the
virtues.[68] I rul'd each page with red ink, so as to have seven
columns, one for each day of the week, marking each column with a
letter for the day. I cross'd these columns with thirteen red lines,
marking the beginning of each line with the first letter of one of the
virtues, on which line, and in its proper column, I might mark, by a
little black spot, every fault I found upon examination to have been
committed respecting that virtue upon that day.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin turns Poor Richard's Almanac into a widely read vehicle for moral instruction, filling it with proverbs about industry, frugality, and virtue, and later condenses those maxims into a celebrated discourse that is widely reprinted and distributed.
anchor_source.first_words: In 1732 I first publish'd my
anchor_source.last_words: observable for several years after its publication.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
In 1732 I first publish'd my Almanack, under the name of _Richard
Saunders_; it was continu'd by me about twenty-five years, commonly
call'd _Poor Richard's Almanac_.[74] I endeavour'd to make it both
entertaining and useful, and it accordingly came to be in such demand,
that I reap'd considerable profit from it, vending annually near ten
thousand. And observing that it was generally read, scarce any
neighborhood in the province being without it, I consider'd it as a
proper vehicle for conveying instruction among the common people, who
bought scarcely any other books; I therefore filled all the little
spaces that occurr'd between the remarkable days in the calendar with
proverbial sentences, chiefly such as inculcated industry and
frugality, as the means of procuring wealth, and thereby securing
virtue; it being more difficult for a man in want, to act always
honestly, as, to use here one of those proverbs, _it is hard for an
empty sack to stand upright_.

    [74] The almanac at that time was a kind of periodical as
    well as a guide to natural phenomena and the weather.
    Franklin took his title from _Poor Robin_, a famous
    English almanac, and from Richard Saunders, a well-known
    almanac publisher. For the maxims of Poor Richard, see
    pages 331-335.

These proverbs, which contained the wisdom of many ages and nations, I
assembled and form'd into a connected discourse prefix'd to the Almanack
of 1757, as the harangue of a wise old man to the people attending an
auction. The bringing all these scatter'd councils thus into a focus
enabled them to make greater impression. The piece, being universally
approved, was copied in all the newspapers of the Continent; reprinted
in Britain on a broadside, to be stuck up in houses; two translations
were made of it in French, and great numbers bought by the clergy and
gentry, to distribute gratis among their poor parishioners and tenants.
In Pennsylvania, as it discouraged useless expense in foreign
superfluities, some thought it had its share of influence in producing
that growing plenty of money which was observable for several years
after its publication.

anchor.note: The scenario matches Franklin’s setup of a widely read annual almanac with blank calendar spaces, and the response faithfully paraphrases that he used those spaces for proverbs promoting industry and frugality because he saw the almanac as an instructional vehicle for readers who bought few other books.

anchor_source.event_description: As a boy, Franklin leads other children in secretly taking stones to build a wharf for fishing, but the theft is discovered and he is corrected by his father, leading him to conclude that usefulness does not justify dishonesty.
anchor_source.first_words: I disliked the trade, and had
anchor_source.last_words: because better instructed, tastes and appetites.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
I disliked the trade, and had a strong inclination for the sea, but my
father declared against it; however, living near the water, I was much
in and about it, learnt early to swim well, and to manage boats; and
when in a boat or canoe with other boys, I was commonly allowed to
govern, especially in any case of difficulty; and upon other occasions
I was generally a leader among the boys, and sometimes led them into
scrapes, of which I will mention one instance, as it shows an early
projecting public spirit, tho' not then justly conducted.

There was a salt-marsh that bounded part of the mill-pond, on the edge
of which, at high water, we used to stand to fish for minnows. By much
trampling, we had made it a mere quagmire. My proposal was to build a
wharf there fit for us to stand upon, and I showed my comrades a large
heap of stones, which were intended for a new house near the marsh,
and which would very well suit our purpose. Accordingly, in the
evening, when the workmen were gone, I assembled a number of my
playfellows, and working with them diligently like so many emmets,
sometimes two or three to a stone, we brought them all away and built
our little wharf. The next morning the workmen were surprised at
missing the stones, which were found in our wharf. Inquiry was made
after the removers; we were discovered and complained of; several of
us were corrected by our fathers; and, though I pleaded the usefulness
of the work, mine convinced me that nothing was useful which was not
honest.

I think you may like to know something of his person and character. He
had an excellent constitution of body, was of middle stature, but well
set, and very strong; he was ingenious, could draw prettily, was
skilled a little in music, and had a clear, pleasing voice, so that
when he played psalm tunes on his violin and sung withal, as he
sometimes did in an evening after the business of the day was over, it
was extremely agreeable to hear. He had a mechanical genius too, and,
on occasion, was very handy in the use of other tradesmen's tools; but
his great excellence lay in a sound understanding and solid judgment
in prudential matters, both in private and publick affairs. In the
latter, indeed, he was never employed, the numerous family he had to
educate and the straitness of his circumstances keeping him close to
his trade; but I remember well his being frequently visited by leading
people, who consulted him for his opinion in affairs of the town or of
the church he belonged to, and showed a good deal of respect for his
judgment and advice: he was also much consulted by private persons
about their affairs when any difficulty occurred, and frequently
chosen an arbitrator between contending parties. At his table he liked
to have, as often as he could, some sensible friend or neighbor to
converse with, and always took care to start some ingenious or useful
topic for discourse, which might tend to improve the minds of his
children. By this means he turned our attention to what was good,
just, and prudent in the conduct of life; and little or no notice was
ever taken of what related to the victuals on the table, whether it
was well or ill dressed, in or out of season, of good or bad flavor,
preferable or inferior to this or that other thing of the kind, so
that I was bro't up in such a perfect inattention to those matters as
to be quite indifferent what kind of food was set before me, and so
unobservant of it, that to this day if I am asked I can scarce tell a
few hours after dinner what I dined upon. This has been a convenience
to me in traveling, where my companions have been sometimes very
unhappy for want of a suitable gratification of their more delicate,
because better instructed, tastes and appetites.
