anchor_source.event_description: Franklin's father rejects Sir William Keith's proposal to set him up in business, judging him too young and inexperienced, though he later encourages Franklin to return to Philadelphia with caution and industry.
anchor_source.first_words: My father received the governor's letter with
anchor_source.last_words: York, now with their approbation and their blessing.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
My father received the governor's letter with some apparent surprise,
but said little of it to me for some days, when Capt. Holmes returning
he show'd it to him, asked him if he knew Keith, and what kind of man
he was; adding his opinion that he must be of small discretion to
think of setting a boy up in business who wanted yet three years of
being at man's estate. Holmes said what he could in favour of the
project, but my father was clear in the impropriety of it, and at
last, gave a flat denial to it. Then he wrote a civil letter to Sir
William, thanking him for the patronage he had so kindly offered me,
but declining to assist me as yet in setting up, I being, in his
opinion, too young to be trusted with the management of a business so
important, and for which the preparation must be so expensive.

My friend and companion Collins, who was a clerk in the post-office,
pleas'd with the account I gave him of my new country, determined to
go thither also; and, while I waited for my father's determination, he
set out before me by land to Rhode Island, leaving his books, which
were a pretty collection of mathematicks and natural philosophy, to
come with mine and me to New York, where he propos'd to wait for me.

My father, tho' he did not approve Sir William's proposition, was yet
pleas'd that I had been able to obtain so advantageous a character
from a person of such note where I had resided, and that I had been so
industrious and careful as to equip myself so handsomely in so short a
time; therefore, seeing no prospect of an accommodation between my
brother and me, he gave his consent to my returning again to
Philadelphia, advis'd me to behave respectfully to the people there,
endeavour to obtain the general esteem, and avoid lampooning and
libeling, to which he thought I had too much inclination; telling me,
that by steady industry and a prudent parsimony I might save enough by
the time I was one-and-twenty to set me up; and that, if I came near
the matter, he would help me out with the rest. This was all I could
obtain, except some small gifts as tokens of his and my mother's love,
when I embark'd again for New York, now with their approbation and
their blessing.

anchor.note: The scenario and action fit the passage: Josiah rejects Keith’s proposal, consents to Franklin’s return to Philadelphia with advice and small gifts, and Franklin departs for New York with parental approval; the added thought is a reasonable inference from 'This was all I could obtain' plus the father's praise, caution, and promise of future help.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin's growing access to books through the library deepens his study habits, while his father’s proverb about diligence becomes a guiding principle linking industry to future distinction.
anchor_source.first_words: This library afforded me the means
anchor_source.last_words: to several hundred pounds in value.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
This library afforded me the means of improvement by constant study,
for which I set apart an hour or two each day, and thus repair'd in
some degree the loss of the learned education my father once intended
for me. Reading was the only amusement I allow'd myself. I spent no
time in taverns, games, or frolicks of any kind; and my industry in
my business continu'd as indefatigable as it was necessary. I was
indebted for my printing-house; I had a young family coming on to be
educated, and I had to contend with for business two printers, who
were established in the place before me. My circumstances, however,
grew daily easier. My original habits of frugality continuing, and my
father having, among his instructions to me when a boy, frequently
repeated a proverb of Solomon, "Seest thou a man diligent in his
calling, he shall stand before kings, he shall not stand before mean
men," I from thence considered industry as a means of obtaining wealth
and distinction, which encourag'd me, tho' I did not think that I
should ever literally _stand before kings_, which, however, has since
happened; for I have stood before _five_, and even had the honor of
sitting down with one, the King of Denmark, to dinner.

We have an English proverb that says, "_He that would thrive, must ask
his wife_." It was lucky for me that I had one as much dispos'd to
industry and frugality as myself. She assisted me chearfully in my
business, folding and stitching pamphlets, tending shop, purchasing
old linen rags for the paper-makers, etc., etc. We kept no idle
servants, our table was plain and simple, our furniture of the
cheapest. For instance, my breakfast was a long time break and milk
(no tea), and I ate it out of a twopenny earthen porringer, with a
pewter spoon. But mark how luxury will enter families, and make a
progress, in spite of principle: being call'd one morning to
breakfast, I found it in a China bowl, with a spoon of silver! They
had been bought for me without my knowledge by my wife, and had cost
her the enormous sum of three-and-twenty shillings, for which she had
no other excuse or apology to make, but that she thought _her_ husband
deserv'd a silver spoon and China bowl as well as any of his
neighbors. This was the first appearance of plate and China in our
house, which afterward, in a course of years, as our wealth increas'd,
augmented gradually to several hundred pounds in value.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin and James increasingly quarrel over apprenticeship duties and authority, and James's beatings leave Franklin resentful and eager to escape the apprenticeship.
anchor_source.first_words: Encourag'd, however, by this, I wrote
anchor_source.last_words: man: perhaps I was too saucy and provoking.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Encourag'd, however, by this, I wrote and conveyed in the same way to
the press several more papers which were equally approv'd; and I kept
my secret till my small fund of sense for such performances was pretty
well exhausted, and then I discovered[24] it, when I began to be
considered a little more by my brother's acquaintance, and in a manner
that did not quite please him, as he thought, probably with reason,
that it tended to make me too vain. And, perhaps, this might be one
occasion of the differences that we began to have about this time.
Though a brother, he considered himself as my master, and me as his
apprentice, and, accordingly, expected the same services from me as he
would from another, while I thought he demean'd me too much in some he
requir'd of me, who from a brother expected more indulgence. Our
 disputes were often brought before our father, and I fancy I was
either generally in the right, or else a better pleader, because the
judgment was generally in my favor. But my brother was passionate,
and had often beaten me, which I took extreamly amiss; and, thinking
my apprenticeship very tedious, I was continually wishing for some
opportunity of shortening it, which at length offered in a manner
unexpected.

    [24] Disclosed.

[Illustration: "I was employed to carry the papers thro' the streets
to the customers"]

One of the pieces in our newspaper on some political point, which I
have now forgotten, gave offense to the Assembly. He was taken up,
censur'd, and imprison'd for a month, by the speaker's warrant, I
suppose, because he would not discover his author. I too was taken up
and examin'd before the council; but, tho' I did not give them any
satisfaction, they contented themselves with admonishing me, and
dismissed me, considering me, perhaps, as an apprentice, who was bound
to keep his master's secrets.

During my brother's confinement, which I resented a good deal,
notwithstanding our private differences, I had the management of the
paper; and I made bold to give our rulers some rubs in it, which my
brother took very kindly, while others began to consider me in an
unfavorable light, as a young genius that had a turn for libeling and
satyr. My brother's discharge was accompany'd with an order of the
House (a very odd one), that "_James Franklin should no longer print
the paper called the New England Courant_."

There was a consultation held in our printing-house among his friends,
what he should do in this case. Some proposed to evade the order by
changing the name of the paper; but my brother, seeing inconveniences
in that, it was finally concluded on as a better way, to let it be
printed for the future under the name of Benjamin Franklin; and to
avoid the censure of the Assembly, that might fall on him as still
printing it by his apprentice, the contrivance was that my old
indenture should be return'd to me, with a full discharge on the back
of it, to be shown on occasion, but to secure to him the benefit of my
service, I was to sign new indentures for the remainder of the term,
which were to be kept private. A very flimsy scheme it was; however,
it was immediately executed, and the paper went on accordingly, under
my name for several months.

At length, a fresh difference arising between my brother and me, I
took upon me to assert my freedom, presuming that he would not venture
to produce the new indentures. It was not fair in me to take this
advantage, and this I therefore reckon one of the first errata of my
life; but the unfairness of it weighed little with me, when under the
impressions of resentment for the blows his passion too often urged
him to bestow upon me, though he was otherwise not an ill-natur'd man:
perhaps I was too saucy and provoking.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
I began now to have some acquaintance among the young people of the
town, that were lovers of reading, with whom I spent my evenings very
pleasantly; and gaining money by my industry and frugality, I lived
very agreeably, forgetting Boston as much as I could, and not desiring
that any there should know where I resided, except my friend Collins,
who was in my secret, and kept it when I wrote to him. At length, an
incident happened that sent me back again much sooner than I had
intended. I had a brother-in-law, Robert Holmes, master of a sloop
that traded between Boston and Delaware. He being at Newcastle, forty
miles below Philadelphia, heard there of me, and wrote me a letter
mentioning the concern of my friends in Boston at my abrupt departure,
assuring me of their good will to me, and that everything would be
accommodated to my mind if I would return, to which he exhorted me
very earnestly. I wrote an answer to his letter, thank'd him for his
advice, but stated my reasons for quitting Boston fully and in such a
light as to convince him I was not so wrong as he had apprehended.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the passage’s Philadelphia setting and Holmes’s appeal from Boston, and the response accurately reflects Franklin’s written reply thanking Holmes and fully justifying his departure; the thought is a fair inference from his wish to forget Boston and keep his residence secret, though 'submit the quarrel to James’s terms' is slightly stronger than the passage explicitly states.

anchor_source.first_words: The breaking into this money of
anchor_source.last_words: did not happen for some years after.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
The breaking into this money of Vernon's was one of the first great
errata of my life; and this affair show'd that my father was not much
out in his judgment when he suppos'd me too young to manage business
of importance. But Sir William, on reading his letter, said he was too
prudent. There was great difference in persons; and discretion did not
always accompany years, nor was youth always without it. "And since he
will not set you up," says he, "I will do it myself. Give me an
inventory of the things necessary to be had from England, and I will
send for them. You shall repay me when you are able; I am resolv'd to
have a good printer here, and I am sure you must succeed." This was
spoken with such an appearance of cordiality, that I had not the least
doubt of his meaning what he said. I had hitherto kept the proposition
of my setting up, a secret in Philadelphia, and I still kept it. Had
it been known that I depended on the governor, probably some friend,
that knew him better, would have advis'd me not to rely on him, as I
afterwards heard it as his known character to be liberal of promises
which he never meant to keep. Yet, unsolicited as he was by me, how
could I think his generous offers insincere? I believ'd him one of the
best men in the world.

I presented him an inventory of a little print'-house, amounting by my
computation to about one hundred pounds sterling. He lik'd it, but
ask'd me if my being on the spot in England to chuse the types, and
see that everything was good of the kind, might not be of some
advantage. "Then," says he, "when there, you may make acquaintances,
and establish correspondences in the bookselling and stationery way."
I agreed that this might be advantageous. "Then," says he, "get
yourself ready to go with Annis;" which was the annual ship, and the
only one at that time usually passing between London and Philadelphia.
But it would be some months before Annis sail'd, so I continued
working with Keimer, fretting about the money Collins had got from me,
and in daily apprehensions of being call'd upon by Vernon, which,
however, did not happen for some years after.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin declines command of the Philadelphia regiment and instead recommends Lawrence, then helps secure cannon and serves as a common soldier at the battery.
anchor_source.first_words: The officers of the companies composing
anchor_source.last_words: if the peace had not soon interven'd.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
The officers of the companies composing the Philadelphia regiment,
being met, chose me for their colonel; but, conceiving myself unfit, I
declin'd that station, and recommended Mr. Lawrence, a fine person,
and man of influence, who was accordingly appointed. I then propos'd a
lottery to defray the expense of building a battery below the town,
and furnishing it with cannon. It filled expeditiously, and the
battery was soon erected, the merlons being fram'd of logs and fill'd
with earth. We bought some old cannon from Boston, but, these not
being sufficient, we wrote to England for more, soliciting, at the
same time, our proprietaries for some assistance, tho' without much
expectation of obtaining it.

Meanwhile, Colonel Lawrence, William Allen, Abram Taylor, Esqr., and
myself were sent to New York by the associators, commission'd to
borrow some cannon of Governor Clinton. He at first refus'd us
peremptorily; but at dinner with his council, where there was great
drinking of Madeira wine, as the custom of that place then was, he
softened by degrees, and said he would lend us six. After a few more
bumpers he advanc'd to ten; and at length he very good-naturedly
conceded eighteen. They were fine cannon, eighteen-pounders, with
their carriages, which we soon transported and mounted on our battery,
where the associators kept a nightly guard while the war lasted, and
among the rest I regularly took my turn of duty there as a common
soldier.

My activity in these operations was agreeable to the governor and
council; they took me into confidence, and I was consulted by them in
every measure wherein their concurrence was thought useful to the
association. Calling in the aid of religion, I propos'd to them the
proclaiming a fast, to promote reformation, and implore the blessing
of Heaven on our undertaking. They embrac'd the motion; but, as it was
the first fast ever thought of in the province, the secretary had no
precedent from which to draw the proclamation. My education in New
England, where a fast is proclaimed every year, was here of some
advantage: I drew it in the accustomed stile, it was translated into
German,[81] printed in both languages, and divulg'd thro' the province.
This gave the clergy of the different sects an opportunity of
influencing their congregations to join in the association, and it
would probably have been general among all but Quakers if the peace
had not soon interven'd.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin marries Miss Read despite legal uncertainties about her previous marriage, and the union proves happy and materially supportive.
anchor_source.first_words: But this affair having turned my
anchor_source.last_words: Blest day that I made her my own.
anchor_source.key_moment: Miss Read's marriage during his absence
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
But this affair having turned my thoughts to marriage, I look'd round
me and made overtures of acquaintance in other places; but soon found
that, the business of a printer being generally thought a poor one, I
was not to expect money with a wife, unless with such a one as I
should not otherwise think agreeable. A friendly correspondence as
neighbours and old acquaintances had continued between me and Mrs.
Read's family, who all had a regard for me from the time of my first
lodging in their house. I was often invited there and consulted in
their affairs, wherein I sometimes was of service. I piti'd poor Miss
Read's unfortunate situation, who was generally dejected, seldom
chearful, and avoided company. I considered my giddiness and
inconstancy when in London as in a great degree the cause of her
unhappiness, tho' the mother was good enough to think the fault more
her own than mine, as she had prevented our marrying before I went
thither, and persuaded the other match in my absence. Our mutual
affection was revived, but there were now great objections to our
union. The match was indeed looked upon as invalid, a preceding wife
being said to be living in England; but this could not easily be
prov'd, because of the distance; and, tho' there was a report of his
death, it was not certain. Then, tho' it should be true, he had left
many debts, which his successor might be call'd upon to pay. We
ventured, however, over all these difficulties, and I took her to
wife, September 1st, 1730. None of the inconveniences happened that we
had apprehended; she proved a good and faithful helpmate,[62] assisted
me much by attending the shop; we throve together, and have ever
mutually endeavour'd to make each other happy. Thus I corrected that
great _erratum_ as well as I could.

    [62] Mrs. Franklin survived her marriage over forty
    years. Franklin's correspondence abounds with evidence
    that their union was a happy one. "We are grown old
    together, and if she has any faults, I am so used to
    them that I don't perceive them." The following is a
    stanza from one of Franklin's own songs written for the
    Junto:

      "Of their Chloes and Phyllises poets may prate,
         I sing my plain country Joan,
       These twelve years my wife, still the joy of my life,
         Blest day that I made her my own."

anchor.note: The scenario accurately reflects Franklin’s renewed closeness with the Read family, Miss Read’s dejection, and the legal-financial objections to union, and the response faithfully paraphrases that he pitied her, blamed his own past inconstancy in part, and nevertheless ventured over the difficulties to marry her, with no invented speech.

weak_pairs.note: Both phases answer by having him marry and accept the risks, with the main difference lying only in thought-style—Phase 1 frames it as repairing past inconstancy, while Phase 2 frames it as settled household partnership.

discrimination.note: P0→P1 is clearly separated because he moves from delaying and leaving the bond unsecured to actively marrying her; P1→P2 is comparatively overlapping on action and commitment level, differing mostly in motivational construal.

probes.scenario: At a crowded railway platform in a mill town, Benjamin Franklin is due to leave on work and spots Miss Read waiting under the timetable board. She says she has heard he may be gone a long while and asks whether she ought to expect letters from him this time.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin respond when Miss Read asks for something plain enough to hold him to?

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin Franklin shifts his bag, smiles awkwardly, and gives her a vague assurance before turning back toward the train.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I'll write when I can. Things are unsettled just now.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He feels the pull of her meaning, but plain promises make him uneasy. It is easier to leave matters soft and trust distance to excuse whatever he fails to do.

voice.note: The awkward evasion, weak promise, and self-excusing inward drift fit Franklin's early neglectful attachment, and the language is plain enough to suit an early-20th-century railway setting without leaking later knowledge.

phase_fit.note: His awkward vagueness and explicit preference to avoid plain promises, letting distance excuse neglect, squarely match the deferred, embarrassed, uncommitted stance of interrupted attachment.

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin Franklin sets his bag down and tells Miss Read where to send word, trying to fix a real understanding before he leaves.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Yes. You shall hear from me, and if I fail, you may call me to account for it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He knows too well what neglect can cost and hears in her question an old wound reopened. This time he wants the bond made by choice, not left to drift or accident.

voice.note: The promise and inward regret fit Franklin's chapter-7 renewed tenderness, and the railway-platform diction stays broadly early-20th-century without importing later knowledge, though the thought is slightly polished for a young man.

phase_fit.note: His thought centers on regret over prior neglect and a deliberate choice to re-enter and secure the bond, which fits the transitional, reparative stance of renewed tenderness more than either early inconstancy or fully settled marriage.

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin Franklin takes Mrs. Franklin's hand and confirms the address and train dates with her in a steady, matter-of-fact way.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You'll have my letter on Sunday, and a wire if plans change.
phase_responses.gt_thought: To him, her asking is not a test but part of keeping a household sure under strain. Reliability is now a form of affection, and being counted on feels like home.

voice.note: The reply fits Franklin’s settled, practical domestic phase: the promise of a Sunday letter and a wire suits the early-20th-century railway setting, and the thought frames affection as dependable household management rather than romantic uncertainty.

phase_fit.note: His thought frames correspondence as routine domestic reliability and emotional home, which fits a settled, maintained marriage rather than regretful or transitional attachment.

world.note: The railway-platform setup and all three phase summaries fit an early-20th-century industrial world with no source-world leakage, keep Benjamin Franklin as protagonist, and present him in the required progression from young adult to settled adult.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are clearly separated on the commitment axis: P0 leaves the bond vague and unattended, P1 explicitly accepts accountability and tries to secure it, and P2 further consolidates that commitment into routine, dependable domestic maintenance.

0.rationale: In chapters 2–5, the emphasis on debate practice, literary exchange, and the sharpening of rhetorical habits fits Franklin and Collins in their teen years, before fully independent adult roles are established.

1.rationale: In chapters 4–6, Collins's debts, drinking, and practical irresponsibility suggest the transition into early independent adulthood, when such behavior creates real social and financial burdens.

2.rationale: By chapter 7, Collins is remembered affectionately but treated as an unreliable cautionary example, which fits Franklin's early adult retrospective judgment after the friendship has failed as dependable support.

probes.scenario: At a coffee-house table, Collins lays down a half-finished sheet and asks Franklin to go over it with him that evening, then to speak for him to a tradesman if he does not appear by morning. He laughs off the uncertainty and waits to see whether Franklin will take the paper and engage him.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin respond to Collins in this moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: He takes the sheet and begins reading, marking a line with his finger.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Come, let us mend the argument first; the rest may settle after.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Collins is good company in such matters, and a rough piece from him is an invitation to exercise my own judgment. I take the request chiefly as another occasion for our useful sparring.

voice.note: The action, speech, and thought fit young Franklin’s early, eager intellectual companionship with Collins, using period-plausible language and no knowledge beyond chapter 3.

phase_fit.note: His thought frames Collins primarily as a stimulating intellectual partner and the request as an occasion for useful debate, with no emphasis on managing irresponsibility or withholding trust.

phase_responses.gt_action: He keeps the sheet in his hand but does not sit; he questions Collins about the morning errand.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I will look on this; but if the man must be answered, you should be there yourself.
phase_responses.gt_thought: I still value his parts, yet every small request threatens to become my burden before it is done. His easy manner puts me on guard, for wit does not pay debts or keep appointments.

voice.note: The caution, practical disappointment, and lingering respect fit Franklin’s chapter-5 view of Collins, and the diction is period-appropriate aside from a slightly polished inward phrasing that still remains plausible.

phase_fit.note: His thought centers on Collins's irresponsibility turning even minor requests into practical burdens, showing ongoing engagement tempered by disappointment rather than full withdrawal of trust.

phase_responses.gt_action: He returns the sheet and declines to undertake the message for him.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I wish you well, Collins, but I must leave your business in your own hands.
phase_responses.gt_thought: I can bear him no ill will, but I no longer build anything upon his promises. To draw close again in work or obligation would be to invite the old disappointment.

voice.note: The refusal is measured, affectionate, and wary in a way that fits Franklin’s diminished trust in Collins by this point, and the language is broadly period-appropriate without reaching beyond chapter 7 knowledge.

phase_fit.note: His thought explicitly shows affectionate feeling without reliance—he keeps Collins at arm’s length because he no longer trusts his promises or treats him as a dependable associate.

world.note: The coffee-house setup, paper draft, and appeal to a tradesman fit Franklin’s early-18th-century world, Collins is an appropriate figure for chapter 3, and the responses reflect the arc without reproducing a specific canonical scene.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are clearly separated on the decision variable: P0→P1 shifts from eager collaborative engagement to guarded, conditional involvement, and P1→P2 shifts from reluctant tolerance to explicit refusal and arm’s-length distance.

probes.scenario: At dusk in the threshing yard, Benjamin Franklin finds John Collins late again for a promised turn of work, smelling of ale while a sharp question about land shares still hangs between them from the last market day. The grain waits under a threatening sky as Collins grins and asks where Benjamin would have him begin.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer Collins in this moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin sets Collins to the flail beside him and keeps the work going while taking up the argument as they labor.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Take the near side, John, and tell me again why the elder son must have the larger share.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Collins's lateness is an annoyance, but not yet a warning. Benjamin still feels the quickening pleasure of meeting him stroke for stroke in talk, and work seems only another place for their contest.

voice.note: The action, speech, and thought fit an adolescent Franklin in the early sparring phase, with period-plausible diction and the right eager, argumentative pleasure that has not yet hardened into distrust.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames Collins's lateness as a minor annoyance rather than a reliability problem, and Franklin still actively seeks him out as an intellectual sparring partner even while they work.

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin gives Collins the lighter task of gathering sheaves and watches whether he will keep to it.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Mind the dry bundles, John, and leave off jesting till the grain is housed.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Benjamin still has warmth for him, but now he measures the cost of that warmth in spoiled labor and mended mistakes. Collins no longer comes as a companion only; he comes with a burden tied to him.

voice.note: The action and speech fit a practical young Franklin managing Collins’s unreliability, and the thought aptly marks the phase’s shift from warm companionship to burdensome disappointment without anachronism or later-arc knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on Collins as an ongoing practical burden whose irresponsibility creates extra work and supervision, which matches the 'moral burden' phase more than either lively sparring or fully withdrawn trust.

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin points Collins to a small edge task apart from the main stack and keeps the central work in his own hands.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Set those loose sheaves under cover there; I will see to the stack.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The old liking remains, yet Benjamin no longer leans on him even for ordinary steadiness. Collins serves now less as help than as a reminder of what wit is worth when character will not bear weight.

voice.note: The response fits Franklin’s cooled, practical distrust of Collins at this stage, and its diction and judgment are broadly period-appropriate, though the thought is slightly polished in phrasing.

phase_fit.note: His thought explicitly says he no longer relies on Collins for even ordinary steadiness and sees him chiefly as a cautionary reminder, which matches diminished trust more than merely managing a troublesome companion.

world.note: The threshing-yard setup and all three phase summaries fit a pre-industrial agrarian world with no source-world leakage, keep Benjamin Franklin as protagonist, and present a plausible progression from adolescent to young-adult attitudes and responsibilities across the required life stages.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are clearly separated on the reliance axis: P0→P1 shifts from treating Collins as an active side-by-side partner in work and argument to managing him as a risky burden, and P1→P2 further shifts from supervised tolerance to explicit arm’s-length assignment and withdrawal of dependence.

probes.scenario: On the way to Philadelphia, Franklin is in a boat on the Delaware with Collins and other young men. Collins, soured by drink and prior quarrels, refuses to row in his turn and presses the matter till the boat stalls in a tense stand-off.

phase_responses.gt_speech: Come, Collins, this is but fair; take your turn.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He still meets Collins as a companion to be reasoned with. The affront feels like a dispute among equals, and he leans toward contest and correction more than estrangement.

voice.note: This fits young Franklin’s early, argumentative camaraderie with Collins: the speech is plain and period-safe, and the thought rightly treats the clash as a fair-minded dispute with an equal rather than the later, more burdened distrust.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames Collins as an equal companion to be argued with and corrected, emphasizing ongoing sparring rather than practical burden or settled distrust.

phase_responses.gt_thought: His mind is already soured by Collins's drinking, debts, and odd behavior. This is no lively sparring now, but the vexing overflow of a friend's misconduct, and he resists being imposed upon again.

voice.note: This fits Franklin in the early moral-burden phase: the action and blunt speech match the boat quarrel, and the thought plausibly frames Collins less as a debating companion than as an increasingly troublesome friend without using anachronistic language or later knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on Collins's drinking, debts, and being a practical imposition, which matches the phase where Franklin still deals with him but chiefly as a burdensome, disappointing companion.

phase_responses.gt_action: He keeps the boat from Collins till the danger of tiring grows plain, then has him taken in, cold and dripping, with little more to say.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Will you row?
phase_responses.gt_thought: He reads Collins less as a friend to reclaim than as a man not to be relied on. Affection is thinned by judgment; he manages the immediate risk, but his esteem is gone.

voice.note: This fits Franklin’s cooled, practical view of Collins at this point—brief, controlled speech and a judgmental inward turn suit the scene, and nothing in the wording feels knowledge-breaking or seriously anachronistic for the episode.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly frames Collins as someone Franklin can no longer rely on and whose esteem is lost, which matches diminished trust more than merely managing a troublesome companion.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
The sloop putting in at Newport, Rhode Island, I visited my brother
John, who had been married and settled there some years. He received
me very affectionately, for he always lov'd me. A friend of his, one
Vernon, having some money due to him in Pennsylvania, about
thirty-five pounds currency, desired I would receive it for him, and
keep it till I had his directions what to remit it in. Accordingly, he
gave me an order. This afterwards occasion'd me a good deal of
uneasiness.

At Newport we took in a number of passengers for New York, among
which were two young women, companions, and a grave, sensible,
matronlike Quaker woman, with her attendants. I had shown an obliging
readiness to do her some little services, which impress'd her I
suppose with a degree of good will toward me; therefore, when she saw
a daily growing familiarity between me and the two young women, which
they appear'd to encourage, she took me aside, and said, "Young man, I
am concern'd for thee, as thou hast no friend with thee, and seems not
to know much of the world, or of the snares youth is expos'd to;
depend upon it, those are very bad women; I can see it in all their
actions; and if thee art not upon thy guard, they will draw thee into
some danger; they are strangers to thee, and I advise thee, in a
friendly concern for thy welfare, to have no acquaintance with them."
As I seem'd at first not to think so ill of them as she did, she
mentioned some things she had observ'd and heard that had escap'd my
notice, but now convinc'd me she was right. I thank'd her for her kind
advice, and promis'd to follow it. When we arriv'd at New York, they
told me where they liv'd, and invited me to come and see them; but I
avoided it, and it was well I did; for the next day the captain miss'd
a silver spoon and some other things, that had been taken out of his
cabin, and, knowing that these were a couple of strumpets, he got a
warrant to search their lodgings, found the stolen goods, and had the
thieves punish'd. So, tho' we had escap'd a sunken rock, which we
scrap'd upon in the passage, I thought this escape of rather more
importance to me.

At New York I found my friend Collins, who had arriv'd there some time
before me. We had been intimate from children, and had read the same
books together; but he had the advantage of more time for reading and
studying, and a wonderful genius for mathematical learning, in which
he far outstript me. While I liv'd in Boston, most of my hours of
leisure for conversation were spent with him, and he continu'd a sober
as well as an industrious lad; was much respected for his learning by
several of the clergy and other gentlemen, and seemed to promise
making a good figure in life. But, during my absence, he had acquir'd
a habit of sotting with brandy; and I found by his own account, and
what I heard from others, that he had been drunk every day since his
arrival at New York, and behav'd very oddly. He had gam'd, too, and
lost his money, so that I was oblig'd to discharge his lodgings, and
defray his expenses to and at Philadelphia, which prov'd extremely
inconvenient to me.

The then governor of New York, Burnet (son of Bishop Burnet), hearing
from the captain that a young man, one of his passengers, had a great
many books, desir'd he would bring me to see him. I waited upon him
accordingly, and should have taken Collins with me but that he was not
sober. The gov'r. treated me with great civility, show'd me his
library, which was a very large one, and we had a good deal of
conversation about books and authors. This was the second governor who
had done me the honour to take notice of me; which, to a poor boy like
me, was very pleasing.

We proceeded to Philadelphia. I received on the way Vernon's money,
without which we could hardly have finish'd our journey. Collins
wished to be employ'd in some counting-house; but, whether they
discover'd his dramming by his breath, or by his behaviour, tho' he
had some recommendations, he met with no success in any application,
and continu'd lodging and boarding at the same house with me, and at
my expense. Knowing I had that money of Vernon's, he was continually
borrowing of me, still promising repayment as soon as he should be in
business. At length he had got so much of it that I was distress'd to
think what I should do in case of being call'd on to remit it.

His drinking continu'd, about which we sometimes quarrel'd; for, when
a little intoxicated, he was very fractious. Once, in a boat on the
Delaware with some other young men, he refused to row in his turn. "I
will be row'd home," says he. "We will not row you," says I. "You
must, or stay all night on the water," says he, "just as you please."
The others said, "Let us row; what signifies it?" But, my mind being
soured with his other conduct, I continu'd to refuse. So he swore he
would make me row, or throw me overboard; and coming along, stepping
on the thwarts, toward me, when he came up and struck at me, I clapped
my hand under his crutch, and, rising, pitched him head-foremost into
the river. I knew he was a good swimmer, and so was under little
concern about him; but before he could get round to lay hold of the
boat, we had with a few strokes pull'd her out of his reach; and ever
when he drew near the boat, we ask'd if he would row, striking a few
strokes to slide her away from him. He was ready to die with
vexation, and obstinately would not promise to row. However, seeing
him at last beginning to tire, we lifted him in and brought him home
dripping wet in the evening. We hardly exchang'd a civil word
afterwards, and a West India captain, who had a commission to procure
a tutor for the sons of a gentleman at Barbados, happening to meet
with him, agreed to carry him thither. He left me then, promising to
remit me the first money he should receive in order to discharge the
debt; but I never heard of him after.

The breaking into this money of Vernon's was one of the first great
errata of my life; and this affair show'd that my father was not much
out in his judgment when he suppos'd me too young to manage business
of importance.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the Delaware boat quarrel with Collins and other young men, the quoted speech and action accurately reflect Franklin’s refusal and his throwing Collins into the river after being struck at, and the thought is supported by the text’s explicit note that Franklin’s mind was 'soured with his other conduct'—his drinking, debts, and odd behavior.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are clearly separated on the decision variable: P0→P1 moves from treating Collins as a disputing equal to resisting and punishing his imposition, and P1→P2 moves from troubled engagement with a burdensome friend to cool, managerial distance toward someone no longer trusted.

probes.scenario: Collins comes to Franklin in some haste, saying he has promised to carry a small packet and a note to a tradesman by evening, but would rather stay and talk at the alehouse; he begs Franklin to take the errand for him, calling it a trifle between friends.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer Collins at that moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: He takes the packet, but pauses to question Collins on why he made a promise he will not keep.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I'll carry it this once; but tell me, Collins, why promise what you mean another should perform?
phase_responses.gt_thought: He still meets Collins as a companion worth engaging, even in a fault. The inconvenience seems a fair price for another bout of reasoning, and perhaps a chance to mend him by argument.

voice.note: The action, speech, and thought fit young Franklin’s early habit of turning even a small inconvenience into a moral and argumentative exercise with Collins, and the diction is suitably period without reaching beyond chapter-3 knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The thought treats Collins primarily as an engaging companion for reasoning and reform through argument, with the inconvenience accepted as secondary rather than as a defining burden or a sign of lost trust.

phase_responses.gt_action: He refuses the packet and presses it back into Collins's hand.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No, Collins; the business is yours, and you must discharge it yourself.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Franklin reads this less as a trifle than one more burden laid on him by Collins's loose conduct. He is tired of paying, carrying, and excusing where Collins should govern himself.

voice.note: The refusal and inward complaint fit Franklin’s chapter-5 disappointment with Collins’s drinking and unreliability, and the diction stays plausibly eighteenth-century without reaching beyond what he yet knows.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on Collins as an ongoing practical and moral burden—Franklin is weary of covering for his irresponsibility—rather than on intellectual companionship or a fully settled withdrawal of trust.

phase_responses.gt_action: He steps aside from the errand and leaves Collins to settle it without him.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I advise you to go about it directly; I cannot undertake it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He no longer treats Collins as a partner whose affairs may safely mingle with his own. The old affection remains, but trust is spent, and he sees more use in keeping clear than in rescuing him again.

voice.note: This fits Franklin at the diminished-trust phase: the refusal is plain and practical, and the thought aptly shows lingering affection joined to a settled resolve not to entangle himself in Collins's unreliable affairs.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly says Franklin no longer mingles Collins's affairs with his own and sees him as someone he cannot safely rely on, which matches diminished trust rather than merely tolerating a burdensome friend.

world.note: The alehouse errand fits the early-18th-century Philadelphia setting and Collins's role in Franklin's life around chapter 5, uses only plausible contemporaneous characters and circumstances, and evokes their dynamic without reproducing a specific canonical scene.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are clearly separated on the reliance/arm’s-length axis: P0→P1 shifts from helping Collins as an engaged companion to refusing to absorb his irresponsibility, and P1→P2 further shifts from weary refusal of a specific burden to a broader stance of non-entanglement grounded in lost trust.

probes.scenario: At a coffee-house table, Collins comes to Franklin with a folded sheet and asks him to carry it to a tradesman with Franklin's recommendation, saying a small loan will set him right and that he will repay within the week. He presses near, confident and familiar, while the room listens for Franklin's answer.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer Collins in that moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: He takes the paper and glances it over, drawing Collins a little aside from the table.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Come, let me see how you have worded it; perhaps it may be mended.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Collins is still a lively companion, and I am apt to meet him in the spirit of amendment and contrivance. I take this first as a matter to be improved by wit and phrasing, not yet as a warning against the man himself.

voice.note: The action and speech fit young Franklin’s habit of treating Collins first as an intellectual companion whose writing may be amended, and the thought stays within chapter-3 knowledge without anachronism, though it is slightly more explicit in self-analysis than Franklin would naturally phrase.

phase_fit.note: His thought frames Collins primarily as a lively intellectual companion whose problem is approached through revision and wit, not as an irresponsible burden or an unreliable man to be kept at arm’s length.

phase_responses.gt_action: He keeps his hands from the paper and lowers his voice, refusing to carry it himself.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No, Collins; I would not engage my name in it. You must settle this by your own care.
phase_responses.gt_thought: I have found his promises light and the burden apt to fall on me. Friendship still pulls, yet I now reckon the inconvenience before the compliment, and I will not be made answerable for his disorder.

voice.note: The refusal is suitably cautious and disappointed for Franklin in this phase, and the diction—'engage my name,' 'answerable,' 'disorder'—fits both the period and his growing sense that Collins's debts and promises are becoming a practical burden.

phase_fit.note: His thought centers on Collins as unreliable and on refusing to make himself answerable for him, which goes beyond mere inconvenience into clear withdrawal of trust and keeping Collins at arm’s length.

phase_responses.gt_action: He declines the errand and turns back to his own company, offering no further help.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I wish you well, Collins, but I shall not meddle in this affair.
phase_responses.gt_thought: I bear him some old affection, but no trust. What once seemed spirit and sociable ease now reads as a claim upon other men's credit, and I will keep him at a safer distance.

voice.note: The refusal fits Franklin’s cooled regard for Collins in this phase, and the diction—especially 'meddle,' 'credit,' and the measured inward judgment—sounds plausibly eighteenth-century without reaching beyond chapter 7.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly contrasts lingering affection with a complete lack of trust and a desire to keep Collins at a safer distance, which most strongly matches diminished trust rather than merely tolerating him as a burden.

world.note: The coffee-house loan request fits the early-18th-century Franklin setting and Collins's role by this point, avoids an exact reproduction of a canonical episode, and the phase summaries remain consistent with the arc's progression from adolescent camaraderie to young-adult distrust.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are clearly separated: P0→P1 shifts from collaborative engagement with Collins and willingness to improve and carry the matter into explicit refusal to risk Franklin’s name, and P1→P2 further shifts from reluctant boundary-setting within friendship to cooler disengagement and greater social distance grounded in outright lack of trust.

probes.scenario: In a monastery scriptorium attached to the governor's court, Benjamin Franklin and John Collins are asked to prepare a clean petition before the noon audience. Collins arrives late, smelling of wine, yet starts arguing brilliantly over the wording while the clerk waits for the finished copy.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin respond with the clerk watching and Collins pressing his point?

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin keeps Collins beside him and revises the petition line by line, answering each objection while urging him back to the text.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If your phrase is stronger, prove it on the page and help me finish.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Collins is troublesome only in the lively way of a sharp companion; the contest itself feels useful. Benjamin values the friction, because it hones his wording and keeps his mind bright.

voice.note: This fits early Franklin well: he keeps Collins as an intellectual sparring partner, the phrasing is broadly period-safe, and the thought reflects adolescent delight in useful debate without importing later disappointment.

phase_fit.note: His thought frames Collins chiefly as a stimulating intellectual foil whose argumentative friction is useful, not as a practical burden or someone no longer trusted.

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin takes the petition into his own hands and sets Collins to copying a short section under his eye.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Save the fine dispute for later; write this part fair and keep steady.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Collins still has wit enough to improve a sentence, but Benjamin now counts the cost of every indulgence. What should be shared labor too often turns into Benjamin's burden to manage.

voice.note: It fits Franklin in this phase: practical, mildly disappointed, still acknowledging Collins’s wit while managing his unreliability, and the diction stays broadly pre-modern without obvious anachronism or later knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on Collins's wit being outweighed by the practical burden of managing his drinking and unreliability, which matches the 'moral burden' phase more than either active sparring or fully diminished trust.

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin finishes the petition himself and gives Collins no part beyond hearing the final wording.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Listen if you like; I will carry this copy to the clerk.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Benjamin no longer mistakes clever talk for sound help. He can still feel old affection, but Collins has become a man to remember kindly and rely on sparingly.

voice.note: The response fits Franklin’s phase of diminished trust—practical, cool, and still faintly affectionate—and its wording is broadly plausible for the era, though the thought is slightly polished in summary style.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly frames Collins as someone Franklin remembers with affection but now relies on only sparingly, which matches diminished trust rather than merely managing a troublesome companion.

world.note: The monastery-court petition scene fits a pre-modern imperial setting without source-world leakage, Benjamin Franklin remains the protagonist, and the three phases plausibly track him from adolescent collaborative sparring to young-adult supervision and then withholding trust.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are clearly separated on the reliance axis: P0→P1 shifts from keeping Collins as an active working partner to supervised, limited participation, and P1→P2 shifts further to excluding Collins from the work as someone not relied upon.

phase_contrasts.contrast: Franklin shifts from engaging Denham chiefly for the practical opportunity he offers to actively trusting and admiring his counsel and reliability in a fatherly way.

0.rationale: In chapter 6, Denham is presented as an established source of employment and practical opportunity, which fits a settled working adult rather than a youth.

1.rationale: In chapter 7, Franklin views Denham as a stabilizing, almost fatherly counselor whose moral seriousness and beneficence suggest an older-adult role.

probes.scenario: At a coffee-house, Mr. Denham finds Franklin over a letter from another gentleman promising introductions and easy advancement, then quietly says such offers often cost more than they seem. He asks to see the letter, and waits while Franklin holds it in his hand.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer Mr. Denham in that pause?

phase_responses.gt_action: He hands Denham the letter and watches his face for judgment.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I should be glad of your opinion, sir; the offer has a fair outside.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Denham seems a sensible man, and more likely to speak plain truth than those who deal in compliments. Franklin values the advice chiefly because it may help him choose the safer, more profitable opening.

voice.note: The action, speech, and thought fit Franklin's early practical regard for Denham as a plain-dealing, useful adviser, with period-appropriate diction and no knowledge beyond chapter 6.

phase_fit.note: His thought frames Denham chiefly as a plain-speaking, useful adviser for choosing the safer, more profitable opportunity, not yet as a fatherly figure he deeply relies on.

phase_responses.gt_action: He gives Denham the letter and leans to hear him, setting his own first opinion aside.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Pray read it, sir; I would rather be guided by your judgment than by fine promises.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Franklin takes Denham's caution as the care of an elder who wishes him well, not mere worldly shrewdness. He looks to him not only for advantage, but for sound direction from a man he can trust.

voice.note: The deference in action, the period-appropriate 'Pray read it, sir,' and the thought of Denham as a trusted elder fit Franklin's chapter-7 regard for him as reliable, morally serious, and almost fatherly rather than merely useful.

phase_fit.note: The thought and speech frame Denham as a trusted elder whose judgment Franklin prefers and relies on, not merely as a practical source of opportunity.

world.note: The coffee-house setting, letter-based patronage talk, and Denham’s presence fit the chapter-6 era and cast, and while the setup echoes Denham’s role as a trustworthy alternative to empty promises, it does not reproduce a specific canonical scene.

discrimination.note: The sole adjacent pair (P0→P1) is separated: both actions are similar, but speech and especially thought shift from valuing Denham as a sensible source of practical advice for safer profit to relying on him as a trusted elder whose judgment and care guide Franklin.

probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin respond to Mr. Denham in this moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin asks Denham for the job details and says he is interested in the position.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If the terms are sound, sir, I’d be glad to hear more.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Denham looks like a man who means what he says, and that already sets him above loud promise-makers. Benjamin reads this first as a solid opening: honest work, clear terms, a way forward.

voice.note: The response fits an adult Franklin in a contemporary diaspora setting: cautious, practical, attentive to clear terms over flashy promises, and it keeps Denham at this phase as a credible work contact rather than yet a fatherly guide.

phase_fit.note: His thought frames Denham chiefly as an honest, practical opening for work with clear terms, not yet as a relied-on elder whose counsel he admires in a fatherly way.

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin sets aside the other offer and asks Denham what course he thinks best.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I trust your judgment here. Tell me how you think I should proceed.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Benjamin hears more than a job offer in Denham’s words; he hears care, steadiness, and a wish to keep him from folly. He leans on that counsel the way one leans on an elder who has earned gratitude and trust.

voice.note: This fits phase 1 well: in a contemporary diaspora setting the language is natural and unanachronistic, and Franklin’s action, speech, and thought all show Denham treated not merely as useful employment but as a trusted, almost fatherly guide.

phase_fit.note: The response goes beyond accepting useful work and explicitly frames Denham as a trusted elder whose steady, caring counsel Benjamin relies on.

probes.scenario: At supper, Mr. Denham hears Franklin speak warmly of a new scheme and answers with a grave caution: the gain may be fair enough, but the men in it are loose in their payments and looser in their word. He leaves the matter with Franklin, saying he may judge for himself.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer Mr. Denham in that moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: He thanks Denham, asks a short question about the men’s credit, and weighs whether the warning alters the advantage.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I am obliged to you, sir; have they failed often in their payments?
phase_responses.gt_thought: Denham seems a sensible man and likelier honest than the common sort of pretenders, so his warning deserves notice. Still, I chiefly consider what this may mean for my employment and prospects.

voice.note: The response fits Franklin’s early, practical regard for Denham as a sensible and comparatively trustworthy source of opportunity, and its diction and concerns are plausible for the period and chapter.

phase_fit.note: His thought treats Denham chiefly as a sensible, honest source of useful warning about business risk, while his main concern remains employment and prospects rather than reliance on Denham as a fatherly guide.

phase_responses.gt_action: He lays the scheme aside for the present and accepts Denham’s caution as enough to govern him.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Then I shall let it rest, sir; your judgment in these matters is safer than my own heat.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He takes Denham’s gravity not as a hindrance but as a kindness, meant to keep him from a foolish step. Denham’s steadiness has become something to lean on, almost as one would on a prudent father.

voice.note: This fits chapter-7 Franklin well: the diction is period-appropriate, the deference to Denham’s steadier judgment matches the deepened, almost fatherly trust of this phase, and nothing reaches beyond what he could yet know.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly frames Denham as a steady, father-like guide whose caution Franklin relies on, which matches the deepened trust phase rather than a merely practical employment connection.

families.axis_name: From emotional susceptibility to critical respect
families.decision_variable: When Whitefield appeals to him, does Franklin act on the immediate emotional pull of Whitefield's rhetoric or keep his own judgment separate and decide independently?

phase_contrasts.contrast: Franklin shifts from yielding behaviorally to Whitefield's emotional appeal by giving money to withholding support and making an independent decision about the orphan-house project.

Franklin shifts from independently disagreeing while still defending Whitefield in practice to stepping back further and treating Whitefield's persuasive power as something to analyze rather than simply respond to.

axis_re_expression.abstract_axis: The balance between emotional receptivity to a compelling other and the preservation of independent evaluative judgment.
abstract_phases: Emotionally swayed into compliant generosity
Independent disagreement with retained trust
Detached respect coupled with analytical appraisal

0.rationale: In chapter 11 Franklin is already an established civic and financial actor who can be swayed into charitable giving by Whitefield's preaching, which fits an adult rather than youthful stage.

1.rationale: Also in chapter 11, Franklin independently evaluates Whitefield's orphan-house scheme, refuses support, and publicly defends his honesty, showing the settled judgment of an adult.

2.rationale: In chapter 11 Franklin's cooler reflection on Whitefield's rhetoric and influence as an object of analysis aligns with a mature adult phase of life.

probes.scenario: At one of George Whitefield's sermons, Franklin has already refused to support the Georgia orphan-house as planned and comes in resolved to give nothing if a collection is made. As Whitefield rises toward his close, the appeal gathers force and the plate is about to pass.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin respond as Whitefield's sermon bears down on his resolution?

phase_responses.gt_action: He yields by degrees and, when the collection comes, empties his pocket into the dish, copper, silver, and gold.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He means to stand firm, yet Whitefield's eloquence works upon him stroke by stroke. Ashamed of giving little and carried by the sermon, he lets the present feeling overrule his prior judgment.

voice.note: This fits Franklin at the 'amazed and moved' phase: the action and thought closely match his chapter-11 susceptibility to Whitefield's rising eloquence, with period-appropriate phrasing and no knowledge beyond the scene.

phase_fit.note: The response shows Franklin's prior independent resolution being overridden by Whitefield's immediate emotional eloquence, culminating in giving money under rhetorical sway.

phase_responses.gt_action: He keeps his money and lets the collector pass, still attending Whitefield civilly and without rancor.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Whitefield's warmth moves him, but he separates the man's sincerity from the soundness of this scheme. He will not buy agreement with a gift; his judgment on the project must remain his own.

voice.note: This fits Franklin's chapter-11 stance: he is moved yet keeps his purse shut, distinguishing Whitefield's sincerity from the prudence of the Georgia scheme in language and judgment plausible to the period and character.

phase_fit.note: He is emotionally moved yet explicitly keeps his judgment separate, refusing to give while preserving respect for Whitefield's sincerity, which matches cordial disagreement rather than susceptibility or detached analysis.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Mr. Whitefield, in leaving us, went preaching all the way thro' the
colonies to Georgia. The settlement of that province had lately been
begun, but, instead of being made with hardy, industrious husbandmen,
accustomed to labour, the only people fit for such an enterprise, it
was with families of broken shop-keepers and other insolvent debtors,
many of indolent and idle habits, taken out of the jails, who, being
set down in the woods, unqualified for clearing land, and unable to
endure the hardships of a new settlement, perished in numbers, leaving
many helpless children unprovided for. The sight of their miserable
situation inspir'd the benevolent heart of Mr. Whitefield with the
idea of building an Orphan House there, in which they might be
supported and educated. Returning northward, he preach'd up this
charity, and made large collections, for his eloquence had a wonderful
power over the hearts and purses of his hearers, of which I myself was
an instance.

I did not disapprove of the design, but, as Georgia was then destitute
of materials and workmen, and it was proposed to send them from
Philadelphia at a great expense, I thought it would have been better
to have built the house here, and brought the children to it. This I
advis'd; but he was resolute in his first project, rejected my
counsel, and I therefore refus'd to contribute. I happened soon after
to attend one of his sermons, in the course of which I perceived he
intended to finish with a collection, and I silently resolved he
should get nothing from me. I had in my pocket a handful of copper
money, three or four silver dollars, and five pistoles in gold. As he
proceeded I began to soften, and concluded to give the coppers.
Another stroke of his oratory made me asham'd of that, and determin'd
me to give the silver; and he finish'd so admirably, that I empty'd my
pocket wholly into the collector's dish, gold and all. At this sermon
there was also one of our club, who, being of my sentiments respecting
the building in Georgia, and suspecting a collection might be
intended, had, by precaution, emptied his pockets before he came from
home. Towards the conclusion of the discourse, however, he felt a
strong desire to give, and apply'd to a neighbour who stood near him,
to borrow some money for the purpose. The application was
unfortunately [made] to perhaps the only man in the company who had
the firmness not to be affected by the preacher. His answer was, "_At
any other time, Friend Hopkinson, I would lend to thee freely; but not
now, for thee seems to be out of thy right senses._"

Some of Mr. Whitefield's enemies affected to suppose that he would
apply these collections to his own private emolument; but I, who was
intimately acquainted with him (being employed in printing his Sermons
and Journals, etc.), never had the least suspicion of his integrity,
but am to this day decidedly of opinion that he was in all his conduct
a perfectly _honest man_; and methinks my testimony in his favour
ought to have the more weight, as we had no religious connection. He
us'd, indeed, sometimes to pray for my conversion, but never had the
satisfaction of believing that his prayers were heard. Ours was a mere
civil friendship, sincere on both sides, and lasted to his death.

anchor_source.last_words: money itself being of a prolific nature.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
By hearing him often, I came to distinguish easily between sermons
newly compos'd, and those which he had often preach'd in the course of
his travels. His delivery of the latter was so improv'd by frequent
repetitions that every accent, every emphasis, every modulation of
voice, was so perfectly well turn'd and well plac'd, that, without
being interested in the subject, one could not help being pleas'd with
the discourse; a pleasure of much the same kind with that receiv'd
from an excellent piece of musick. This is an advantage itinerant
preachers have over those who are stationary, as the latter cannot
well improve their delivery of a sermon by so many rehearsals.

His writing and printing from time to time gave great advantage to his
enemies; unguarded expressions, and even erroneous opinions, delivered
in preaching, might have been afterwards explain'd or qualifi'd by
supposing others that might have accompani'd them, or they might have
been deny'd; but _litera scripta manet_. Critics attack'd his writings
violently, and with so much appearance of reason as to diminish the
number of his votaries and prevent their increase; so that I am of
opinion if he had never written anything, he would have left behind
him a much more numerous and important sect, and his reputation might
in that case have been still growing, even after his death, as there
being nothing of his writing on which to found a censure and give him
a lower character, his proselytes would be left at liberty to feign
for him as great a variety of excellences as their enthusiastic
admiration might wish him to have possessed.

My business was now continually augmenting, and my circumstances
growing daily easier, my newspaper having become very profitable, as
being for a time almost the only one in this and the neighbouring
provinces. I experienced, too, the truth of the observation, "_that
after getting the first hundred pound, it is more easy to get the
second_," money itself being of a prolific nature.

anchor.note: The scenario and response faithfully match Franklin’s reflective analysis here: he compares Whitefield’s new versus oft-repeated sermons, praises the polished effect of repeated delivery, and concludes that Whitefield’s writing/printing gave critics grounds to diminish his following, with no invented speech or action.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin negotiates with the proprietaries over the Pennsylvania tax act, ultimately making a written assurance that the proprietary estate will not be injured by its execution. The Assembly praises him for securing the law's passage, but the proprietaries remain enraged and hostile.
anchor_source.first_words: But during this delay, the Assembly
anchor_source.last_words: the threats and they were never
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
But during this delay, the Assembly having prevailed with Gov'r Denny
to pass an act taxing the proprietary estate in common with the
estates of the people, which was the grand point in dispute, they
omitted answering the message.

When this act however came over, the proprietaries, counselled by
Paris, determined to oppose its receiving the royal assent.
Accordingly they petitioned the king in Council, and a hearing was
appointed in which two lawyers were employ'd by them against the act,
and two by me in support of it. They alledg'd that the act was
intended to load the proprietary estate in order to spare those of the
people, and that if it were suffer'd to continue in force, and the
proprietaries, who were in odium with the people, left to their mercy
in proportioning the taxes, they would inevitably be ruined. We
reply'd that the act had no such intention, and would have no such
effect. That the assessors were honest and discreet men under an oath
to assess fairly and equitably, and that any advantage each of them
might expect in lessening his own tax by augmenting that of the
proprietaries was too trifling to induce them to perjure themselves.
This is the purport of what I remember as urged by both sides, except
that we insisted strongly on the mischievous consequences that must
attend a repeal, for that the money, £100,000, being printed and given
to the king's use, expended in his service, and now spread among the
people, the repeal would strike it dead in their hands to the ruin of
many, and the total discouragement of future grants, and the
selfishness of the proprietors in soliciting such a general
catastrophe, merely from a groundless fear of their estate being taxed
too highly, was insisted on in the strongest terms. On this, Lord
Mansfield, one of the counsel, rose, and beckoning me took me into the
clerk's chamber, while the lawyers were pleading, and asked me if I
was really of opinion that no injury would be done the proprietary
estate in the execution of the act. I said certainly. "Then," says he,
"you can have little objection to enter into an engagement to assure
that point." I answer'd, "None at all." He then call'd in Paris, and
after some discourse, his lordship's proposition was accepted on both
sides; a paper to the purpose was drawn up by the Clerk of the
Council, which I sign'd with Mr. Charles, who was also an Agent of the
Province for their ordinary affairs, when Lord Mansfield returned to
the Council Chamber, where finally the law was allowed to pass. Some
changes were however recommended and we also engaged they should be
made by a subsequent law, but the Assembly did not think them
necessary; for one year's tax having been levied by the act before the
order of Council arrived, they appointed a committee to examine the
proceedings of the assessors, and on this committee they put several
particular friends of the proprietaries. After a full enquiry, they
unanimously sign'd a report that they found the tax had been assess'd
with perfect equity.

The Assembly looked into my entering into the first part of the
engagement, as an essential service to the Province, since it secured
the credit of the paper money then spread over all the country. They
gave me their thanks in form when I return'd. But the proprietaries
were enraged at Governor Denny for having pass'd the act, and turn'd
him out with threats of suing him for breach of instructions which he
had given bond to observe. He, however, having done it at the instance
of the General, and for His Majesty's service, and having some
powerful interest at court, despis'd the threats and they were never
put in execution.... [unfinished]

anchor.note: The scenario matches the Council hearing, Franklin does answer Lord Mansfield that he has 'None at all' objection, then signs the Clerk's paper and helps secure the act, and the stated thought is supported by the passage's emphasis on preventing repeal and preserving the paper money's credit.

probes.scenario: At a private meeting, a proprietary agent says the Assembly's supply bill may pass if a clause is softened and Franklin will privately assure the House not to press the disputed point again this session. He adds that such compliance would be remembered kindly by the family.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer this offer?

phase_responses.gt_action: He asks the proposal in writing and offers narrower language that saves the money bill while leaving the Assembly's claim untouched.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Put the terms on paper, and perhaps we may mend the wording without hurting the service.
phase_responses.gt_thought: If the public business can be carried by careful wording and a clear reservation, it is worth trying. Proprietary stiffness may be managed by forms, securities, and a little contrivance.

voice.note: This fits Franklin's early pragmatic posture: the request for written terms, the effort to preserve the money bill by narrowing language, and the thought that proprietary obstruction may be managed by forms and contrivance all sound apt to chapter 17 and free of anachronism.

phase_responses.gt_action: He declines the private assurance and says he will report the condition openly to the House.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I make no secret bargains. If there is a condition, let it appear where all may judge it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: This is not a mere stumble of temper but the old design: public measures clogged by hidden instructions and private influence. To yield in private would feed the mischief at its root.

voice.note: The refusal of a private assurance, the insistence on open conditions before the House, and the thought that hidden instructions are the standing source of mischief all fit Franklin's chapter-17 phase and use era-appropriate, character-appropriate language.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is his thought that hidden instructions and private influence are the recurring root of the conflict, which matches seeing proprietary obstruction as a standing structure rather than an isolated negotiable episode.

phase_responses.gt_action: He rejects the offer plainly and leaves the promised favor untouched, carrying the matter back as a proprietary encroachment.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I serve the public, not the family's pleasure; keep your kindness for those who can be bought by it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Their favor is part of the engine by which they would make dependence do the work of reason. Better an open breach than to seem a man who trims the people's rights for patronage.

voice.note: This fits Franklin's late-phase principled refusal of proprietary favor, and while the phrasing is somewhat sharpened for effect, its language and reasoning remain plausible to his era and to chapter 19.

phase_fit.note: He not only treats proprietary favor as structurally corrupting, but explicitly refuses patronage and frames his stance as public duty over private inducement, which is the hallmark of open principled opposition.

anchor_source.event_description: Franklin identifies the root cause of the recurring quarrels as the proprietaries' selfish instructions, which force governors to resist necessary taxation unless their own estates are exempted. He notes that the Assemblies resisted this injustice for years before yielding.
anchor_source.first_words: These public quarrels[94] were all at
anchor_source.last_words: during the administration of Governor Morris.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
These public quarrels[94] were all at bottom owing to the
proprietaries, our hereditary governors, who, when any expense was to
be incurred for the defense of their province, with incredible
meanness instructed their deputies to pass no act for levying the
necessary taxes, unless their vast estates were in the same act
expressly excused; and they had even taken bonds of these deputies to
observe such instructions. The Assemblies for three years held out
against this injustice, tho' constrained to bend at last. At length
Captain Denny, who was Governor Morris's successor, ventured to
disobey those instructions; how that was brought about I shall show
hereafter.

    [93] The "round, selfish, and self-important" squire of
    Don Quixote in Cervantes' romance of that name.

    [94] My acts in Morris's time, military, etc.--_Marg.
    note_.

But I am got forward too fast with my story: there are still some
transactions to be mention'd that happened during the administration
of Governor Morris.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the Pennsylvania tax quarrel setup, and the response faithfully paraphrases Franklin’s narration that the conflicts were fundamentally caused by proprietary instructions selfishly exempting their estates from defense taxes, with the thought reasonably inferred from his explicit judgment.
