anchor_source.event_description: Governor Denny arrives with the Royal Society medal and privately courts Franklin's friendship, hinting at rewards if Franklin will help restore harmony between the governor and the proprietary interest. Franklin declines any proprietary favor, asserts his financial independence, and frames his political stance as principled rather than self-interested.
anchor_source.first_words: Our new governor, Captain Denny, brought over
anchor_source.last_words: but his prose was thought as good
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Our new governor, Captain Denny, brought over for me the
before mentioned medal from the Royal Society, which he presented to
me at an entertainment given him by the city. He accompanied it with
very polite expressions of his esteem for me, having, as he said, been
long acquainted with my character. After dinner, when the company, as
was customary at that time, were engag'd in drinking, he took me aside
into another room, and acquainted me that he had been advis'd by his
friends in England to cultivate a friendship with me, as one who was
capable of giving him the best advice, and of contributing most
effectually to the making his administration easy; that he therefore
desired of all things to have a good understanding with me, and he
begged me to be assured of his readiness on all occasions to render me
every service that might be in his power. He said much to me, also, of
the proprietor's good disposition towards the province, and of the
advantage it might be to us all, and to me in particular, if the
opposition that had been so long continu'd to his measures was dropt,
and harmony restor'd between him and the people; in effecting which,
it was thought no one could be more serviceable than myself; and I
might depend on adequate acknowledgments and recompenses, etc., etc.
The drinkers, finding we did not return immediately to the table, sent
us a decanter of Madeira, which the governor made liberal use of, and
in proportion became more profuse of his solicitations and promises.

My answers were to this purpose: that my circumstances, thanks to God,
were such as to make proprietary favours unnecessary to me; and that,
being a member of the Assembly, I could not possibly accept of any;
that, however, I had no personal enmity to the proprietary, and that,
whenever the public measures he propos'd should appear to be for the
good of the people, no one should espouse and forward them more
zealously than myself; my past opposition having been founded on this,
that the measures which had been urged were evidently intended to
serve the proprietary interest, with great prejudice to that of the
people; that I was much obliged to him (the governor) for his
professions of regard to me, and that he might rely on everything in
my power to make his administration as easy as possible, hoping at the
same time that he had not brought with him the same unfortunate
instruction his predecessor had been hampered with.

On this he did not then explain himself; but when he afterwards came
to do business with the Assembly, they appear'd again, the disputes
were renewed, and I was as active as ever in the opposition, being the
penman, first, of the request to have a communication of the
instructions, and then of the remarks upon them, which may be found in
the votes of the time, and in the Historical Review I afterward
publish'd. But between us personally no enmity arose; we were often
together; he was a man of letters, had seen much of the world, and was
very entertaining and pleasing in conversation. He gave me the first
information that my old friend Jas. Ralph was still alive; that he was
esteem'd one of the best political writers in England; had been
employed in the dispute[111] between Prince Frederic and the king, and
had obtain'd a pension of three hundred a year; that his reputation
was indeed small as a poet, Pope having damned his poetry in the

probes.scenario: At a private supper after Assembly business, an agent for the Proprietaries praises Franklin's usefulness and says a small place of profit could be found for a friend of his if Franklin will soften a pending remonstrance and carry up a more temperate message. The room grows still, and the agent waits for his answer.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin answer this offer in the moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: He asks the agent to put any assurances in writing and shifts the talk to what public clauses may yet be carried.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If they mean fairness, let it appear in plain articles, and public business may still go forward.
phase_responses.gt_thought: An offer of favor is troublesome, yet it may be turned to account if it yields something certain for the province. Better to bind them to terms than spend heat on affront.

voice.note: This fits Franklin's pragmatic, procedural temper at this stage: he neither grandstands nor accepts the inducement, but seeks written terms and a workable public compromise in language plausible to the period.

phase_fit.note: The thought treats proprietary favor as something to convert into concrete written concessions for public business, showing compromise-minded bargaining rather than structural or principled refusal.

phase_responses.gt_action: He declines the personal hint and answers with a cool warning that the remonstrance stands upon the Proprietaries' own instructions.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I serve no interest by halves; mend the instructions, and the complaint will mend with them.
phase_responses.gt_thought: This is not a stray indiscretion but the old engine at work: private advantage set against public measures. The bait matters less than the design behind it, which confirms where the mischief lies.

voice.note: The reply fits Franklin's chapter-17 stance by coolly rejecting inducement and locating the quarrel in proprietary instructions as a standing system of obstruction, with era-appropriate diction and no knowledge beyond this phase.

phase_fit.note: The thought treats the offer as evidence of a recurring system—'the old engine at work'—and locates the conflict in proprietary instructions themselves, which is most diagnostic of structural antagonism rather than mere bargaining or the fully explicit public-principled refusal of patronage.

phase_responses.gt_action: He rejects the overture openly and leaves the remonstrance untouched, refusing any favor tied to his conduct.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I cannot accept obligations from men whose measures I must oppose for the country's sake.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Any favor from them would be taken for purchase, and perhaps would half-purchase a weaker man. My safety is to stand clear of their benefits and let my conduct rest on the public good alone.

voice.note: This fits Franklin’s late-phase public-spirited independence: the refusal of patronage, suspicion that favor would be construed as purchase, and plain 18th-century phrasing all suit his stance and the chapter-19 setting.

phase_fit.note: The response explicitly refuses proprietary patronage and frames that refusal as necessary to preserve independent, public-spirited opposition, which is the hallmark of open principled opposition.

world.note: The supper-and-overture setup fits mid-18th-century Pennsylvania politics, uses only plausible contemporaries and no anachronisms or magic, avoids reproducing a specific canonical scene while remaining faithful to chapter-19-era tensions, and the phase responses consistently portray Franklin as the same older adult at this point in his life.

probes.scenario: At a city relief board meeting, Benjamin Franklin presents a plan to fund a public clinic after a mill accident. A representative of Proprietaries offers support only if Franklin signs a private pledge exempting their company land and keeps the terms out of the minutes.
probes.question: How does Benjamin Franklin respond when Proprietaries ties public aid to a private understanding?

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin Franklin drafts a revised clause offering temporary exemption with a written sunset and full entry in the record.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Put it in writing, plain enough for every man at this table to answer for.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The clinic matters more than winning a point. If Proprietaries can be bound by careful wording and open procedure, public business may yet be saved.

voice.note: This fits Franklin’s pragmatic, procedure-minded phase well: the action, plain public-facing speech, and thought all favor compromise through written safeguards and open record without invoking later principled refusal or any clear era-breaking diction.

phase_fit.note: He is still trying to salvage public business through compromise, careful wording, and transparent procedure, rather than treating proprietary obstruction as a principled adversarial structure to resist outright.

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin Franklin refuses the private pledge and asks that Proprietaries' condition be read aloud into the meeting record.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let the condition stand in the minutes, and then we shall see what sort of bargain this is.
phase_responses.gt_thought: This is not a stray difficulty but the same old engine at work: public need used as leverage for private shelter. Once hidden terms are admitted, every measure will be hamstrung in the same fashion.

voice.note: The response fits Franklin’s phase-1 stance by treating the proprietaries’ demand as evidence of a recurring structural abuse rather than an isolated quarrel, and its diction is broadly plausible for an early-20th-century civic meeting without leaking later-phase knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The thought treats the proprietaries' demand as a recurring structural mechanism of obstruction rather than an isolated negotiable problem, but it stops short of explicitly framing refusal as a public principle against patronage.

phase_responses.gt_action: Benjamin Franklin declines their support outright and submits the clinic plan without Proprietaries' favor.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Keep your favor. The public shall not buy its own safety by serving your exemption.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Their money is meant to tame opposition, not aid the injured. If he takes it on such terms, he becomes their instrument; better to stand clear and oppose them in the open.

voice.note: The refusal of secret favorable terms and the framing of independence as service to the public fit Franklin’s end-phase principled opposition, and the language is broadly plausible for an older Franklin in an early-20th-century civic setting without clear anachronism.

phase_fit.note: He not only sees proprietary aid as structurally corrupting but explicitly refuses their favor and frames open opposition as the principled public course.

world.note: The scenario and all three phase responses fit an early-20th-century civic-industrial setting without source-world leakage, keep Benjamin Franklin as the protagonist, and consistently portray him as an older adult acting in age-appropriate public leadership roles.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are clearly separated: P0→P1 shifts from salvage-through-transparent compromise to exposing and resisting a recurring proprietary tactic, and P1→P2 shifts from recording and contesting the condition to outright refusal of proprietary favor on public principle.
